I-93 runs in tunnel beneath the Greenway on the neighborhood's western edge.

places.name: Paul Revere House
places.line: Built no later than 1680 at 19 North Square and owned by Revere from 1770 to 1800, the oldest residential building still standing in downtown Boston; open to the public since April 18, 1908, operated by the Paul Revere Memorial Association, and a National Historic Landmark since 1961.

places.name: Old North Church (Christ Church)
places.line: At 193 Salem Street, established in 1723 and the oldest church building in Boston, where two lanterns were hung in the steeple on April 18, 1775.

places.name: Copp's Hill Burying Ground
places.line: A two-acre burying ground established in 1659, where Increase and Cotton Mather, Prince Hall and Robert Newman are buried; listed on the National Register on April 18, 1974.

places.name: Paul Revere Mall (the Prado)
places.line: A brick-walled corridor created in 1933 between Hanover Street and Old North Church, with an equestrian statue of Paul Revere.

places.name: Langone Park and Puopolo Playground
places.line: A 4.5-acre city park on Boston Harbor, rebuilt with a Little League field, a multisport field, a playground, bocce and basketball courts, an integrated seawall and a harborwalk raised four feet.

places.name: Rose Kennedy Greenway North End Parks
places.line: Two parcels of the 17-acre Greenway, on either side of Hanover Street, with fountains, lawns and a pergola, on land freed by the demolition of the elevated Central Artery.

places.name: Christopher Columbus Waterfront Park
places.line: A public park on the North End waterfront, one of the neighborhood's green spaces along with Langone Park.

history.text: A fire on November 27 destroyed Increase Mather's house, the North Meeting House and 45 buildings; the Paul Revere House was built on the Mather site no later than 1680.
On April 18, Robert Newman and John Pulling hung two lanterns in the steeple of Old North Church to warn that British troops were crossing the Charles River.
On January 15, a molasses tank at 529 Commercial Street burst, killing 21 people and injuring 150; the tank's site is now Langone Park.
The Rose Fitzgerald Kennedy Greenway opened in October on the site of the elevated Central Artery, which had separated the North End from downtown since the 1950s.

ot_record.name: Charlestown
headline: Red-brick rows on Breed's Hill,
and a navy yard turned to new uses on the harbor.
ot_record.answer: Charlestown is Boston's oldest neighborhood, founded in 1629 on a peninsula between the Charles and Mystic Rivers and annexed to Boston in 1874, with 19,120 residents in 2020 (2020 Census, Boston Planning Department tabulation). Its housing is largely red-brick row houses on Bunker Hill and Breed's Hill, plus buildings of the former Navy Yard converted to residential and other uses. The Orange Line stops at Community College and Sullivan Square, and the MBTA's Charlestown Ferry runs from the Navy Yard to Long Wharf.
ot_record.meta: Charlestown, Boston: founded 1629, red-brick rows on Breed's Hill, the Bunker Hill Monument and Navy Yard, Orange Line and ferry. 2025 Warren Group prices.

boundaries.text: A peninsula north of the Charles River, opposite downtown Boston, bordered by the Mystic River and Boston Harbor, with I-93 along its western edge, the Navy Yard on the harbor, and Sullivan Square where the Charlestown Neck once joined it to the mainland.

overview: Charlestown was laid out by Thomas Graves and settled in 1629, and the City of Boston calls it the city's oldest neighborhood; John Winthrop's company stopped here in 1630 before crossing the Charles River to found Boston. On June 17, 1775, the Battle of Bunker Hill was fought on Breed's Hill, and British forces burned almost the whole town. The first bridge to Boston opened in 1786, and the Navy Yard opened in 1800. Charlestown voters approved annexation on October 7, 1873, by 2,240 to 1,947, and it became part of Boston on January 5, 1874.

The peninsula rises to two small hills, Bunker Hill to the north and Breed's Hill, both covered mostly in housing, much of it red-brick row houses. The 221-foot granite Bunker Hill Monument, reached by 294 steps, was dedicated on Breed's Hill in 1843. City Square, in the southern part of the neighborhood, was the site of the city hall before annexation, and Sullivan Square sits where landfill erased the narrow Charlestown Neck. The Navy Yard closed on July 1, 1974; the National Park Service holds 25 acres as part of Boston National Historical Park, and most of the redeveloped buildings were converted to office, commercial and residential use. The Orange Line has run through Charlestown since April 7, 1975, when Community College and Sullivan Square stations replaced the City Square and Thompson Square stations of the Charlestown Elevated, which had opened in 1901.

Two large changes are under way. The Bunker Hill Housing redevelopment, a partnership of the Boston Housing Authority, the Joseph J. Corcoran Company, Leggat McCall and the Charlestown Resident Alliance, is replacing 1,100 public housing units with 2,699 public, income-restricted and market-rate rental units, with 73,000 square feet of retail and civic space; its first building broke ground in June 2023, and the next, a nine-story building of 265 units, was expected to start in mid to late 2025. On September 28, 2023, after four years of work, the Boston Planning & Development Agency board adopted PLAN: Charlestown, which sets out how new growth can fit along the Rutherford Avenue corridor and in Sullivan Square and proposes new zoning to allow more housing and retail in existing industrial areas.

housing.text: Charlestown's housing stock is largely red-brick row houses, many near the waterfront, along with homes in converted Navy Yard buildings and the Bunker Hill public housing now being rebuilt. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2014 to 2018 American Community Survey counts 9,536 housing units, 9,050 of them occupied; 46.1% of occupied units were owner occupied and 53.9% renter occupied.

areas.name: Charlestown Navy Yard
areas.line: The former naval shipyard on the harbor, open from 1800 to 1974; 25 acres are part of Boston National Historical Park and most of the rest has been redeveloped for office, commercial and residential use.

areas.name: Monument Square and Breed's Hill
areas.line: The hilltop around the Bunker Hill Monument, whose museum stands at 43 Monument Square.

areas.name: City Square
areas.line: In the southern part of the neighborhood, the site of the city hall before annexation; US 1 passes below City Square and Paul Revere Park.

areas.name: Sullivan Square
areas.line: Where the Charlestown Neck once met the mainland, with an Orange Line station and busway; one of the focus areas of PLAN: Charlestown, adopted by the Boston Planning & Development Agency board on September 28, 2023.

commute.text: The Orange Line stops at Community College, on Austin Street beneath the I-93 viaduct, and at Sullivan Square, which has a busway; routes 92 and 93 run from Sullivan Square to downtown. The MBTA's Charlestown Ferry links the Navy Yard with Long Wharf. Charlestown has no commuter rail station. I-93 and US 1, by way of the Tobin Bridge, pass through.

places.name: Bunker Hill Monument
places.line: A 221-foot granite obelisk on Breed's Hill marking the battle of June 17, 1775, dedicated in 1843 and climbed by a spiral stair of 294 steps.

places.name: USS Constitution
places.line: Launched in 1797 and known as Old Ironsides, the world's oldest commissioned warship still afloat, usually berthed at Pier 1 of the Navy Yard and open to visitors year round with free tours.

places.name: USS Cassin Young
places.line: A Fletcher-class destroyer that served from 1943 to 1960, berthed at the Navy Yard, which the National Park Service stewards in partnership with the U.S. Navy and the USS Constitution Museum; the Navy Yard grounds are open 24 hours a day.

places.name: Paul Revere Park
places.line: A five-acre park along the Charles River between the Freedom Trail and the Zakim Bunker Hill Bridge, built as Big Dig mitigation and first opened in 1999.

places.name: Phipps Street Burying Ground
places.line: A 1.8-acre burial ground created in 1630, where John Harvard is buried; listed on the National Register in 1974.

places.name: Winthrop Square (Training Field)
places.line: A historic park and former militia training field, home to the Charlestown Civil War Memorial.

history.text: Thomas Graves laid out Charlestown, settled that year.
The Battle of Bunker Hill was fought on June 17, and British forces burned almost all of the town.
Charlestown was annexed to Boston on January 5, 1874, after voters approved it 2,240 to 1,947.
The Charlestown Navy Yard was deactivated on July 1, 1974, after 174 years.

communities.title: East Boston
communities.excerpt: East Boston is a Boston neighborhood across Boston Harbor from downtown, built on several former islands joined by landfill and laid out on a street grid by the East Boston Company in the 1830s.

ot_record.name: East Boston
headline: Former harbor islands joined by landfill,
with five Blue Line stops, Piers Park and Logan Airport on the water.
ot_record.answer: East Boston is a Boston neighborhood across Boston Harbor from downtown, built on several former islands joined by landfill and laid out on a street grid by the East Boston Company in the 1830s. The Boston Planning Department counted 43,066 residents there in 2020. Its housing runs from Greek Revival brick bowfront houses of 1847 to about 1852 on Jeffries Point to Italianate and Second Empire houses on Eagle Hill, and the Blue Line stops at Maverick, Airport, Wood Island, Orient Heights and Suffolk Downs.
ot_record.meta: East Boston: former harbor islands laid out on a grid from 1833, with Jeffries Point and Eagle Hill, five Blue Line stops, Piers Park and 2025 Warren Group prices.

boundaries.text: East Boston lies across Boston Harbor from downtown and Charlestown and borders Winthrop, Revere and Chelsea. Logan International Airport lies mainly in East Boston, with part of the airfield in Winthrop.

overview: East Boston was built on Noddle's Island, the largest of five islands (with Hog, Governor's, Bird and Apple) that landfill had joined into one landmass, including the ground under Logan Airport, by the 1940s. The island was farmed through the 1700s. By 1833 William H. Sumner, with Steven White and Francis J. Oliver, had bought up half of it, and by 1834 their East Boston Company controlled the island and laid it out on a grid of streets, the first planned neighborhood in Boston. Donald McKay opened his shipyard on Border Street in 1845, and his clipper Flying Cloud (1851) twice sailed from New York to San Francisco in 89 days. Shipbuilding became the mainstay of the local economy.

The oldest streets are on Jeffries Point, at the southern end facing downtown, where Belmont Square (now Brophy Memorial Park) on Camp Hill survives from the original plan and is edged by brick bowfront houses built around 1847 to 1852. Eagle Hill has a National Register historic district of houses built roughly between 1834 and 1900. Maverick Square and Central Square are the main commercial areas. Transportation reshaped the neighborhood through the 20th century: the East Boston streetcar tunnel, now the Blue Line, opened in 1904 as the first underwater tunnel in North America; the airfield that became Logan opened on September 8, 1923; and rows of houses were cleared for the Sumner Tunnel (opened June 30, 1934) and the Callahan Tunnel (1961). The Ted Williams Tunnel brought I-90 to East Boston in 1995.

Recent planning has covered both the established neighborhood and its largest open site. The Boston Planning & Development Agency board adopted PLAN: East Boston on January 18, 2024, after work that began in 2018; it covers roughly two square miles, excluding Logan Airport and the Suffolk Downs site, and the zoning amendments to Article 53 that carry it out were adopted by the Boston Zoning Commission on April 24, 2024. At the former Suffolk Downs racetrack, whose last day of live racing was June 30, 2019, the agency approved in September 2020 a redevelopment of the 161-acre site in East Boston and Revere with 10,000 housing units and almost three million square feet of office and retail space. On the waterfront, Massport opened a 4.5-acre second phase of Piers Park in December 2023.

housing.text: East Boston's housing includes Greek Revival brick bowfront houses of about 1847 to 1852 on Belmont Square, Greek Revival, Italianate and mansard double houses on Jeffries Point (where most residential building came between 1840 and 1890), and Italianate, Second Empire and Renaissance Revival houses in the Eagle Hill historic district. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 17,123 occupied housing units, 25.6% of them owner-occupied and 74.4% renter-occupied.

areas.name: Jeffries Point
areas.line: The earliest-settled part of East Boston, at the southern end facing downtown, developed by the East Boston Company in the 1830s; nine Greek Revival brick bowfront houses at 177 to 193 Webster Street line Belmont Square (Brophy Memorial Park) on Camp Hill.

areas.name: Eagle Hill
areas.line: A National Register historic district, listed on February 26, 1998, roughly bounded by Meridian, Princeton and White Streets meeting in Prescott Square, with mostly Italianate, Second Empire and Renaissance Revival buildings from about 1834 to 1900.

areas.name: Maverick Square
areas.line: One of East Boston's two main commercial areas, with Central Square, and the site of the Blue Line's Maverick station, opened on April 18, 1924.

areas.name: Orient Heights
areas.line: The section of East Boston around Constitution Beach, across the water from the runways of Logan Airport, and the Orient Heights Blue Line station, opened on January 5, 1952.

commute.text: The Blue Line runs under the harbor from Maverick to downtown and stops at five stations in East Boston: Maverick, Airport, Wood Island, Orient Heights and Suffolk Downs. Massport runs free shuttle buses from Airport station to the Logan terminals. The MBTA's seasonal East Boston Ferry links Lewis Mall with Long Wharf. East Boston has no commuter rail station. I-90 reaches it through the Ted Williams Tunnel, and Route 1A through the Sumner and Callahan Tunnels.

places.name: Piers Park
places.line: A Massport park on the southwest side of East Boston facing downtown: the 6.5-acre first phase opened in 1995 with a 600-foot brick promenade, four shade pavilions (one dedicated to Donald McKay) and the Piers Park Sailing Center, and a 4.5-acre second phase opened in December 2023.

places.name: Belle Isle Marsh Reservation
places.line: A DCR reservation at 1399 Bennington Street, described by DCR as Boston's largest remaining salt marsh, with accessible trails.

places.name: Constitution Beach
places.line: A public beach in Orient Heights with a bathhouse, snack bar, playground, courts, baseball fields and an indoor ice rink, about 2,000 feet from Logan's runways 22L and 22R.

places.name: East Boston Greenway
places.line: A path on a former Grand Junction Railroad freight line, opened in 2007, linking Piers Park, Memorial Stadium, Bremen Street Park, Wood Island Bay Marsh and Belle Isle Marsh; it is planned to run 3.3 miles when complete.

places.name: Bremen Street Park
places.line: A park on the Greenway with an entrance to the Blue Line's Airport station.

places.name: Belmont Square (Brophy Memorial Park)
places.line: A square at the top of Camp Hill, developed by the East Boston Company in the 1830s, with views of Boston Harbor, Greek Revival bowfront houses on Webster Street, and the Golden Stairs descending to Marginal Street at the water's edge.

places.name: Donald McKay House
places.line: The shipbuilder's house on White Street, a Boston Landmark since 1977 and listed on the National Register; it is a private residence.

history.text: By this year William H. Sumner, Steven White and Francis J. Oliver had bought up half of Noddle's Island; by 1834 their East Boston Company controlled it and laid it out on a street grid.
Donald McKay opened his shipyard on Border Street, and his ships included the clipper Flying Cloud (1851).
The East Boston streetcar tunnel, now part of the Blue Line, opened on December 30 under the harbor.

communities.title: Jamaica Plain
communities.excerpt: Jamaica Plain is a Boston neighborhood of 4.4 square miles between Jamaica Pond and Franklin Park, part of the town of West Roxbury until it was annexed to Boston in 1874.

ot_record.name: Jamaica Plain
headline: A kettle pond, an arboretum and a cemetery park,
with the Orange Line running under a linear park.
ot_record.answer: Jamaica Plain is a Boston neighborhood of 4.4 square miles between Jamaica Pond and Franklin Park, part of the town of West Roxbury until it was annexed to Boston in 1874. Its housing runs from triple-deckers built from the 1870s onward to Victorian houses on former estates such as Sumner Hill. The Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 41,012 people there in 2020. Four Orange Line stations run under the Southwest Corridor Park, and the Needham Line stops at Forest Hills.
ot_record.meta: Jamaica Plain, Boston: triple-deckers and Victorian houses between Jamaica Pond and Franklin Park, with four Orange Line stops and the Needham Line.

boundaries.text: Jamaica Plain, originally part of Roxbury, meets Roxbury at Egleston Square. Its sections run from Pondside, by Jamaica Pond and the Jamaicaway, and Parkside, beside Franklin Park, south to Forest Hills, near the Arnold Arboretum and Forest Hills Cemetery.

overview: Settlement south of Parker Hill began shortly after 1630, when Boston and Roxbury were founded, and the name Jamaica first appears on maps in the late 1650s. In 1676 John Ruggles and Hugh Thomas gave land for the community's first school, later the Eliot School. From 1795 to 1886, the Jamaica Pond Aqueduct Corporation supplied water from the pond to Boston, Roxbury and later West Roxbury. The Boston and Providence Rail Road arrived in 1834, and in 1851 estate owners here helped split from Roxbury to form the town of West Roxbury, which voted to join Boston in 1873; annexation took effect in 1874. Breweries opened too: Highland Spring on Heath Street from 1867 and Haffenreffer, near Boylston and Amory Streets, from 1871 until 1964.

Triple-deckers first appeared in the 1870s and spread quickly in the 1890s. Larger houses went up on former estates: Sumner Hill on the Greenough land, Parley Vale and Robinwood Avenue in the 1880s, and Moss Hill and Woodland Road on Bowditch family land in the 1890s. By the early 20th century most buildable lots were filled. Much of the neighborhood's edge is parkland in Frederick Law Olmsted's Emerald Necklace: Olmsted Park and Jamaica Pond along the Jamaicaway, the Arnold Arboretum and the Arborway in the south, and Franklin Park beside the Parkside section; the 1848 Forest Hills Cemetery is in the Forest Hills section.

In 1969 Governor Francis Sargent cancelled a planned extension of I-95 through the area after community opposition. The cleared land became the Southwest Corridor: the Orange Line moved from the elevated Washington Street line into a below-grade cut in May 1987, and the park above it was completed in 1990. On March 2, 2017, the Boston Planning & Development Agency board adopted PLAN: JP/ROX, guidelines for about 250 acres between Forest Hills, Egleston Square and Jackson Square, generally bounded by Washington Street, Columbus Avenue and Amory Street, covering housing, jobs, urban design and transportation.

housing.text: Jamaica Plain's housing mixes wood-frame triple-deckers, built from the 1870s and especially in the 1890s, with late-19th-century single-family houses on former estates such as Sumner Hill and Moss Hill. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 18,129 occupied housing units in the neighborhood, 45.6% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: The Monument and Centre Street
areas.line: The area around the intersection of Centre and South Streets, named for the Soldiers' Monument there; the 1760 Loring-Greenough House stands on Monument Square at 12 South Street.

areas.name: Hyde Square
areas.line: The area around Centre, Day and Perkins Streets, extending east along Centre Street toward Roxbury.

areas.name: Jackson Square and Egleston Square
areas.line: Squares at the northern edge, on Columbus Avenue and Washington Street at the Roxbury line; Jackson Square has an Orange Line station, and both fall within the PLAN: JP/ROX study area.

areas.name: Forest Hills
areas.line: The section roughly bounded by the Arborway, Morton Street, Walk Hill Street, South Street and Forest Hills Cemetery, with Forest Hills station at Washington Street and Hyde Park Avenue, rebuilt in 1987 for the Orange Line and commuter rail.

commute.text: The Orange Line runs below street level through Jamaica Plain to Back Bay and downtown, and Forest Hills station, at Washington Street and Hyde Park Avenue, is also a Needham Line commuter rail stop and the terminal for 16 MBTA bus routes. The Green Line E branch ends at Heath Street, and the 39 bus is the neighborhood's main bus route. The Southwest Corridor Park carries a bike path beside the Orange Line, and the Jamaicaway and Arborway run along the Emerald Necklace.

places.name: Jamaica Pond
places.line: A spring-fed glacial kettle hole more than 50 feet deep, taken into the park system in 1891, with a boathouse and bandstand from 1912 and boat rentals in summer.

places.name: Arnold Arboretum
places.line: A 281-acre preserve founded in 1872 and part of the Emerald Necklace, open free every day.

places.name: Franklin Park
places.line: Olmsted's 485-acre park, Boston's largest open space, with the Franklin Park Zoo, White Stadium and the William J. Devine Golf Course; it connects Jamaica Plain with Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan and Roslindale.

places.name: Forest Hills Cemetery
places.line: A garden cemetery founded in 1848 as Roxbury's municipal cemetery and designed by Henry A. S. Dearborn, entered from Morton Street; it was added to the National Register in 2004.

places.name: Loring-Greenough House
places.line: A 1760 country house at 12 South Street, owned since 1924 by the Jamaica Plain Tuesday Club and designated a Boston Landmark in 1999.

places.name: Southwest Corridor Park
places.line: A linear park managed by DCR from Back Bay station to Forest Hills, built over the Orange Line on land cleared for a cancelled highway; its first segments opened in 1987.

places.name: Haffenreffer Brewery buildings
places.line: The former Haffenreffer brewery near Boylston and Amory Streets, which brewed from 1871 until 1964; the old buildings now house the Boston Beer Company, brewer of Samuel Adams.

history.text: John Ruggles and Hugh Thomas donated land for the community's first school, later named the Eliot School.
Jamaica Plain became part of the new town of West Roxbury, set off from Roxbury.
Annexation to Boston took effect after West Roxbury voters approved it in 1873.
The rebuilt Forest Hills station opened on May 4, and Orange Line trains began running through the Southwest Corridor on May 7, replacing the elevated line on Washington Street.

communities.title: Roslindale
communities.excerpt: Roslindale is a Boston neighborhood about six miles south-southwest of downtown, between the Arnold Arboretum and the George Wright Golf Course, and was part of the town of West Roxbury until annexation to Boston took effect in 1874.

ot_record.name: Roslindale
headline: A 1911 substation on the square,
the Needham Line and the Arboretum's Peters Hill.
ot_record.answer: Roslindale is a Boston neighborhood about six miles south-southwest of downtown, between the Arnold Arboretum and the George Wright Golf Course, and was part of the town of West Roxbury until annexation to Boston took effect in 1874. One- and two-family houses make up much of its housing, with newer apartment buildings around Roslindale Square. The Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 29,386 people there in 2020, and the Needham Line stops at Roslindale Village.
ot_record.meta: Roslindale, Boston: one- and two-family houses around Roslindale Square, the Needham Line at Roslindale Village, and the Arnold Arboretum's Peters Hill.

boundaries.text: Boston's open space plan notes that Roslindale's edges are not distinct, but describes the planning district as bounded by the Arnold Arboretum and the Walter Street Tract to the north, the former Boston State Hospital campus and the Forest Hills and Mount Hope cemeteries to the east, the West Roxbury Parkway to the west, and the George Wright Golf Course and part of the Stony Brook Reservation to the south. Jamaica Plain, Hyde Park, West Roxbury and Mattapan are its neighbors.

overview: Roslindale was part of the town of Roxbury until 1851, when it, Jamaica Plain and West Roxbury left Roxbury to form the town of West Roxbury. The Boston and Providence Railroad opened its West Roxbury Branch from Forest Hills to Dedham on July 14, 1849, with a station at South Street, and by the 1860s the area was known as South Street Crossing. When residents sought their own post office district, the government rejected that name, and John Pierce proposed Roslindale, after Roslin, near Edinburgh. Voters approved annexation to Boston in 1873, and it took effect in 1874. Horse-drawn street railway service between Forest Hills and Dedham followed in the 1880s.

Washington Street runs through Roslindale Square, which took its present layout in the 1920s around Adams Park. In the square stands the Roslindale Substation, built for the Boston Elevated Railway in 1911 to a design by Robert S. Peabody and listed on the National Register in 2013. In 1929 Ashland Street, by then widened, was renamed Cummins Highway, from Washington Street to River Street. Roslindale Village Main Street, established in 1985 as one of the first urban Main Street programs in the country, runs the farmers' market and events in the square. To the north, the part of the Arnold Arboretum south of Bussey Street, including Peters Hill, at 240 feet, lies in Roslindale, and rail lines divide the neighborhood roughly into thirds.

Boston's 2008-2014 open space plan counted one- and two-family houses as 60% of Roslindale's housing, against 32% citywide; the western streets resemble West Roxbury, while the northern streets mix two- and three-family houses with light industrial buildings. Roslindale Square was the first plan adopted under the city's Squares + Streets initiative: the planning process ran from February 2024 to February 2025, the Boston Planning & Development Agency board adopted the Roslindale Square Small Area Plan on February 13, 2025, and the Zoning Commission approved new zoning in May 2025, effective June 2, 2025. It was the second area of the city with Squares + Streets districts in force, and the zoning allows multifamily housing near and above ground-floor businesses.

housing.text: Roslindale is mostly one- and two-family houses: Boston's 2008-2014 open space plan put single-family homes at 33% and two-family homes at 27% of units, 60% together, compared with 32% citywide. Its western streets are mainly one- and two-family houses, its northern streets have more two- and three-family houses, and newer apartment buildings stand around Roslindale Square. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 53.8% of occupied units as owner-occupied (6,539 units), compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: Roslindale Square
areas.line: The business district around Adams Park, where Washington Street runs through the square, with Roslindale Village station at 1 Belgrade Avenue, the 1911 Roslindale Substation and the Squares + Streets zoning adopted in 2025.

areas.name: The Arboretum edge
areas.line: The northern side, where the part of the Arnold Arboretum south of Bussey Street, including 240-foot Peters Hill, lies within Roslindale; the 1887 Bussey Street bridge collapse took place on what is now Arboretum land.

areas.name: Cummins Highway
areas.line: Formerly Ashland Street, which had been widened to 60 to 80 feet before it was renamed in 1929; it runs from Washington Street to River Street and was the first road in Boston called a highway.

commute.text: Roslindale Village station, at 1 Belgrade Avenue in the square, is on the Needham Line, which runs through Forest Hills, Ruggles and Back Bay to South Station; Forest Hills, in Jamaica Plain, connects with the Orange Line. Ten MBTA bus routes run on Washington Street between Forest Hills and Roslindale Square and fan out to the south and west. The West Roxbury Parkway runs along the western edge.

places.name: Roslindale Substation
places.line: A 1911 Boston Elevated Railway substation at 4228 Washington Street, designed by Robert S. Peabody of Peabody and Stearns and listed on the National Register on August 27, 2013; the city sold it in 2013 to Historic Boston Incorporated and Roslindale Village Main Street, and its ground floor opened as a beer hall in spring 2022.

places.name: Adams Park
places.line: The green at the center of Roslindale Square, renovated by the city with a performance space, walkways and landscaping; Roslindale Village Main Street's farmers' market has been held there on Saturdays.

places.name: Arnold Arboretum and Peters Hill
places.line: Harvard's 281-acre arboretum, founded in 1872 and open free every day, lies in Jamaica Plain and Roslindale; Peters Hill, at 240 feet the tallest of its hills, is in the Roslindale section.

places.name: Roslindale Wetlands
places.line: A city urban wild, once called the Eldon Street Urban Wild, with a wetland, woodland and meadow, a perimeter loop trail built in improvements between 2020 and 2024, and entrances on Walter Street, Weld Street, Hazelmere Road and Coniston Road.

places.name: Healy Playground and Fallon Field
places.line: City recreation grounds: Healy Playground has three ball fields and a stairway on Washington Street, and Fallon Field has a playground, two basketball courts and a street hockey court.

places.name: George Wright Golf Course
places.line: An 18-hole municipal course designed by Donald Ross and opened on April 23, 1938, at 420 West Street; it lies in Hyde Park and Roslindale and marks Roslindale's southern edge.

history.text: The Boston and Providence Railroad's West Roxbury Branch opened on July 14 with a station at South Street, today's Roslindale Village station.
Annexation to Boston took effect, after voters in the town of West Roxbury, which included Roslindale, approved it in 1873.
On March 14, a railroad bridge at Bussey Street collapsed under a train carrying more than 200 passengers, killing 23; the site is now in the Arnold Arboretum.
The Roslindale Square Small Area Plan, the first plan adopted under Squares + Streets, was adopted on February 13, and its zoning took effect on June 2.

communities.title: West Roxbury
communities.excerpt: West Roxbury is Boston's southwestern neighborhood, bordering Brookline, Newton, Needham and Dedham, set off from Roxbury as its own town in 1851 and annexed to Boston in 1874.

ot_record.name: West Roxbury
headline: Centre Street, three Needham Line stops,
and Bellevue Hill, the city's highest natural point.
ot_record.answer: West Roxbury is Boston's southwestern neighborhood, bordering Brookline, Newton, Needham and Dedham, set off from Roxbury as its own town in 1851 and annexed to Boston in 1874. Its housing is mostly single-family homes with some two-family houses, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 31,561 people there in 2020. Three Needham Line stations, Bellevue, Highland and West Roxbury, run to South Station, and Centre Street is the main business district.
ot_record.meta: West Roxbury, Boston: mostly single-family homes along Centre Street, three Needham Line stations, Millennium Park and Bellevue Hill, the city's highest point.

boundaries.text: West Roxbury is the southwest corner of Boston: Roslindale and Jamaica Plain lie to the northeast, Chestnut Hill and Brookline to the north, Newton to the northwest, Dedham and Needham to the southwest, and Hyde Park to the southeast; VFW Parkway runs along its western side.

overview: West Roxbury was settled in 1630 as farmland, part of the town of Roxbury, and the Westerly Burying Ground on Centre Street dates to 1683. In 1841 George and Sophia Ripley founded Brook Farm, a transcendentalist community, at the Ellis Farm on what is now Baker Street; Nathaniel Hawthorne's stay there became The Blithedale Romance. The Boston and Providence Railroad opened its West Roxbury Branch from Forest Hills to Dedham in 1849, and on May 24, 1851, West Roxbury, then including Jamaica Plain, was incorporated as a separate town. It became part of Boston on January 5, 1874.

Centre Street is the spine of the neighborhood and its business district, with the Theodore Parker Church, a Boston Landmark whose present building dates from 1900, and the Westerly Burying Ground along it. Bellevue Hill, bounded roughly by LaGrange Street, Centre Street and the West Roxbury Parkway, rises to 330 feet, the highest natural point in Boston and Suffolk County, and carries the Bellevue Standpipe. In 1906 the New Haven Railroad extended the branch from West Roxbury to Needham Junction, the route of today's Needham Line.

Open land frames the streets. Boston's 2008-2014 Open Space Plan counted 645 acres of protected open space in West Roxbury, among them the 105-acre Millennium Park, built on the former Gardner Street landfill with material excavated for the Big Dig and opened on December 7, 2000, and Allandale Woods, which the plan called the city's largest urban wild. The 616-acre Stony Brook Reservation runs south from Washington Street in West Roxbury into Hyde Park, and Brook Farm, where the state bought 148 acres of the original land in 1988, is operated by DCR as a historic site.

housing.text: West Roxbury is mostly single-family homes, with some two-family houses. Boston's 2008-2014 Open Space Plan put single-family homes at about 55% of year-round housing units and noted that over three-quarters of units were built after 1920. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 13,868 occupied housing units, 61.7% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: Centre Street
areas.line: The main commercial street and business district, running the length of the neighborhood past the Theodore Parker Church and the Westerly Burying Ground.

areas.name: Bellevue Hill
areas.line: Streets on the city's highest natural point, at 330 feet, bounded roughly by LaGrange Street, Centre Street and the West Roxbury Parkway, with the Bellevue Standpipe on the summit.

areas.name: The Charles River edge
areas.line: The western side along VFW Parkway, with Millennium Park and its canoe launch on the Charles River, Brook Farm on Baker Street, and a VA hospital near the Dedham line.

commute.text: The Needham Line stops at Bellevue, Highland and West Roxbury, at 450 LaGrange Street, and runs through Roslindale Village, Forest Hills, Ruggles and Back Bay to South Station. Forest Hills, at the Jamaica Plain end of the line, connects with the Orange Line. Several MBTA bus routes run through or end in the neighborhood, and VFW Parkway and the West Roxbury Parkway are its main parkways.

places.name: Millennium Park
places.line: A park on the former Gardner Street landfill, reclaimed with material excavated for the Big Dig and opened in 2000; the city's open space plan lists 105 acres, with 21 acres of playing fields and a canoe launch on the Charles River.

places.name: Stony Brook Reservation
places.line: A 616-acre DCR reservation, one of the five original reservations of the Metropolitan Park Commission, running south from Washington Street in West Roxbury to Mother Brook in Hyde Park, with hiking and biking trails and fishing at Turtle Pond.

places.name: Brook Farm
places.line: Site of the 1841 to 1847 transcendentalist community at 670 Baker Street, a National Historic Landmark since 1965, operated by DCR as a historic site.

places.name: Westerly Burying Ground
places.line: A burying ground on Centre Street, at LaGrange Street, dating to 1683, Boston's seventh-oldest cemetery, listed on the National Register in 1987.

places.name: Theodore Parker Church
places.line: A Boston Landmark on Centre Street, its 1900 building designed by Henry Seaver, with seven Tiffany Studios windows; the original 1890 church by Alexander Wadsworth Longfellow Jr. is now the parish hall.

places.name: Allandale Woods
places.line: A wooded city urban wild at the neighborhood's northern edge, described in Boston's open space plan as the city's largest.

history.text: The Westerly Burying Ground was established, when West Roxbury was still part of Roxbury.
George and Sophia Ripley founded the Brook Farm community at the Ellis Farm; it had closed by 1847.
West Roxbury was incorporated as a town on May 24, separate from Roxbury.
West Roxbury became part of Boston on January 5.

communities.title: Hyde Park
communities.excerpt: Hyde Park is Boston's southernmost neighborhood, 7.9 miles south of downtown, incorporated as a town in 1868 from parts of Dorchester, Dedham and Milton and annexed to Boston in 1912.

ot_record.name: Hyde Park
headline: Three commuter rail lines, Mother Brook
and the Neponset River at the city's southern edge.
ot_record.answer: Hyde Park is Boston's southernmost neighborhood, 7.9 miles south of downtown, incorporated as a town in 1868 from parts of Dorchester, Dedham and Milton and annexed to Boston in 1912. Single-family and two-family homes made up nearly three-quarters of its housing units in the city's open space plan, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 33,009 people there in 2020. Three commuter rail lines stop at its Hyde Park, Fairmount and Readville stations.
ot_record.meta: Hyde Park, Boston: a former town with Cleary Square, Victorian Fairmount Hill and Readville, three commuter rail lines and the Stony Brook Reservation.

boundaries.text: Hyde Park is Boston's southernmost neighborhood. The George Wright Golf Course lies partly in Hyde Park and partly in Roslindale, the Stony Brook Reservation runs south from West Roxbury to Mother Brook in Hyde Park, and the city's open space plan places Hyde Park's eastern sections next to Mattapan. In Readville it meets Milton to the south and Dedham to the west. Hyde Park Avenue and the Amtrak and MBTA tracks cross the neighborhood, with most of its open space to their west.

overview: Hyde Park was assembled from the edges of three older towns: Grew's Woods in Dorchester, Fairmount in Milton and Readville in Dedham. Mother Brook, ordered dug in 1639 to divert Charles River water to the Neponset, powered mills in what is now Readville, which was called Dedham Low Plains until 1847, when it was renamed for James Read of the Dedham Manufacturing Company. Henry Grew settled there in 1847, rail lines extended from Boston in the 1850s, and in 1856 Alpheus P. Blake's Fairmount Land Company and Twenty Associates bought 100 acres and began building houses. On April 22, 1868, the Town of Hyde Park was incorporated in Norfolk County from about 1,300 acres of Dorchester, 800 of Dedham and 700 of Milton. Its voters chose to join Boston in 1912.

Cleary Square and Logan Square frame the central business district, and the Hyde Park Branch Library, which opened in its present building in September 1899 and became a Boston Public Library branch at annexation, is the only branch that began as a town library. Fairmount Hill, on a hillside above the Neponset River, keeps late-19th- and early-20th-century houses in Italianate, Gothic Revival and Victorian styles. Readville was industrial: Camp Meigs trained Union regiments there from 1862 to 1865, including the 54th Massachusetts; the Readville Trotting Park followed on the site until 1937; the B.F. Sturtevant Company had a 20-acre plant employing 1,500 people by 1912; and the New Haven Railroad's locomotive and car shops ran until 1960.

Boston's 2008-2014 open space plan counted single-family homes as 48% of Hyde Park's housing units and two-family homes as 24%, and found most of its open space west of Hyde Park Avenue and the rail line; the state Department of Conservation and Recreation held 470 acres in the neighborhood, mainly in the Stony Brook and Neponset River reservations. A rezoning begun in April 2008 was approved by the Boston Zoning Commission in February 2012. Cleary Square is now the subject of a Squares + Streets small area plan: the Planning Department released a draft plan and zoning map on March 17, 2026, followed by a revised draft.

housing.text: Hyde Park's housing is mainly single-family and two-family homes: Boston's 2008-2014 open space plan put single-family homes at 48% of units and two-family homes at 24%, nearly three-quarters together. Fairmount Hill keeps houses in late-19th- and early-20th-century styles, including Italianate, Gothic Revival and Victorian. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 59.5% of occupied units as owner-occupied (7,893 units), compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: Cleary Square and Logan Square
areas.line: The two squares between which Hyde Park's central business district lies; Cleary Square is the focus of a draft Squares + Streets plan released in 2026.

areas.name: Fairmount Hill
areas.line: A hillside above the Neponset River, laid out from 1856 by the Fairmount Land Company, with late-19th- and early-20th-century Italianate, Gothic Revival and Victorian houses; Fairmount station sits at Fairmount Avenue and the Truman Highway.

areas.name: Readville
areas.line: The southern section, formerly Dedham Low Plains, bordered by Milton and Dedham, with Wolcott Square, Readville station at 1800 Hyde Park Avenue, a commuter rail maintenance and layover yard, and the Neponset River and Fowl Meadow wetlands.

commute.text: The Fairmount Line runs from Readville through Fairmount and six more stops to South Station, and Fairmount station is in fare zone 1A. Hyde Park station, at 1 Pingree Street and reached by ramps from the River Street bridge, is a Providence/Stoughton Line stop with some Franklin/Foxboro trains, running to Ruggles, Back Bay and South Station; Readville, at 1800 Hyde Park Avenue, is the outer terminus for most Fairmount trains and a Franklin/Foxboro stop. MBTA bus routes connect the neighborhood with the subway at Forest Hills and Mattapan.

places.name: Stony Brook Reservation
places.line: A 616-acre DCR reservation, one of the five original reservations of the Metropolitan Park Commission, running south from Washington Street in West Roxbury to Mother Brook in Hyde Park, with hiking and biking trails, fishing at Turtle Pond and an ice rink.

places.name: George Wright Golf Course
places.line: An 18-hole City of Boston course designed by Donald Ross and opened on April 23, 1938, at 420 West Street, on 156 acres enclosed by a stone wall.

places.name: Mother Brook
places.line: A canal ordered by Dedham in 1639 and flowing by 1641, about 3.6 miles long, carrying Charles River water to the Neponset River in Hyde Park; the page calls it the first man-made canal in the present-day United States, and it now forms part of a flood-control system.

places.name: Camp Meigs Park
places.line: A park of nearly three acres at 11 Stanbro Street in Readville, on part of the Civil War training camp, dedicated by the Commonwealth on July 11, 1903, with a cannon-shaped granite monument and a later marker to the regiments that trained there, among them the 54th and 55th Massachusetts Infantry and 5th Massachusetts Cavalry.

places.name: Hyde Park Branch Library
places.line: Opened in its present building in September 1899 as the town library, which had started in 1873; it joined the Boston Public Library at annexation in 1912, and a January 2000 addition by Schwartz/Silver Architects doubled its size.

places.name: Neponset River Reservation
places.line: DCR land along the Neponset River, which runs past Readville and below Fairmount Hill; with Stony Brook, it accounts for most of the 470 acres the state holds in the neighborhood.

history.text: Dedham ordered Mother Brook dug to carry Charles River water to the Neponset; water was flowing by July 1641.
The Fairmount Land Company and Twenty Associates bought 100 acres and started their first house on May 15.
The Town of Hyde Park was incorporated on April 22 from parts of Dorchester, Dedham and Milton.
Hyde Park voters chose to join the City of Boston, and the town library became a Boston Public Library branch.

communities.title: Roxbury
communities.excerpt: Roxbury is a Boston neighborhood that the city's planning department describes as the geographic heart of Boston, settled in 1630 and annexed to Boston in 1868.

ot_record.name: Roxbury
headline: A puddingstone hill with an 1869 standpipe tower,
row houses and triple-deckers around Nubian Square.
ot_record.answer: Roxbury is a Boston neighborhood that the city's planning department describes as the geographic heart of Boston, settled in 1630 and annexed to Boston in 1868. Its housing runs from Greek Revival and Italianate houses on Fort Hill to brick row houses and triple-deckers, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 54,905 people there in 2020. The Silver Line runs on Washington Street from Nubian Square, and the Orange Line and commuter rail stop at Ruggles.
ot_record.meta: Roxbury, Boston: Fort Hill's Greek Revival houses, row houses and triple-deckers around Nubian Square, with the Silver Line, the Orange Line and Franklin Park.

boundaries.text: Roxbury sits at the center of Boston: Columbia Road separates it from Dorchester, Franklin Park is divided between Roxbury and Jamaica Plain along Walnut Avenue and Sigourney Street, and Ruggles station stands where Roxbury, the Fenway and Mission Hill meet. Melnea Cass Boulevard runs roughly over the line of the old Roxbury Canal.

overview: Roxbury was settled on September 28, 1630. William Pynchon, one of the founders, left in 1636 with a group of the town's men to found Springfield. The town's houses were set on Roxbury puddingstone, a conglomerate quarried for foundations. Several 18th-century buildings survive: Governor William Shirley built the Shirley-Eustis House as a summer house between 1747 and 1751, and the Dillaway-Thomas House, built as a parsonage about 1750, served as a Continental Army headquarters during the Siege of Boston in 1775. Roxbury became a city in 1846, part of it was set off as the town of West Roxbury in 1851, and Boston annexed the rest on January 5, 1868.

Row houses and multi-family buildings followed trolley service, which began in 1887, and the Washington Street Elevated reached Dudley Square, now Nubian Square, on June 10, 1901. The building stock shows each period. On Fort Hill, around Highland Park, Greek Revival and Italianate houses that predate the Civil War stand among triple-deckers and row houses, below an 1869 standpipe tower built for Roxbury's water system. The Moreland Street district was built up between about 1840 and 1920 with Second Empire, Italianate and Queen Anne houses, and in Lower Roxbury the Tremont Improvement Company built row houses on filled salt marsh around what became Frederick Douglass Square in 1917.

The last train ran on the Washington Street Elevated on April 30, 1987, and the Orange Line moved to the Southwest Corridor, with new stations at Ruggles and Roxbury Crossing opening on May 4. Silver Line buses began running on Washington Street on July 20, 2002. The Boston Planning & Development Agency started PLAN: Dudley Square in 2016 to guide public and vacant parcels around the square, and its board approved the plan's development guidelines on July 11, 2019. On December 19, 2019, the city's Public Improvement Commission renamed Dudley Square as Nubian Square, and in 2022 the city designated the Highland Park Architectural Conservation District, about 170 acres of steep, puddingstone-studded land also called Roxbury Highlands or Fort Hill.

housing.text: The Boston Planning Department describes Roxbury's housing as historic brick row houses and Boston's traditional triple-deckers; Fort Hill adds Greek Revival, Italianate and later Victorian houses, and Cedar Street has a run of 1871 Second Empire row houses. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 20,681 occupied housing units in Roxbury, 26.1% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: Nubian Square
areas.line: The commercial center formerly called Dudley Square, framed by Washington Street, Malcolm X Boulevard, Dudley Street and Guild Row, with Nubian station, the Silver Line terminus and a large MBTA bus terminal, and the Ferdinand Building, now Boston Public Schools headquarters.

areas.name: Fort Hill (Highland Park)
areas.line: A 0.4-square-mile hill bounded by Malcolm X Boulevard, Washington Street and Columbus Avenue, named for a Revolutionary War earthwork; listed on the National Register as the Roxbury Highlands Historic District on February 22, 1989, it holds Greek Revival and Italianate houses, triple-deckers and row houses, and John Eliot Square with the First Church and the Dillaway-Thomas House.

areas.name: Moreland Street Historic District
areas.line: A 63-acre, mainly residential district roughly bounded by Kearsarge and Blue Hill Avenues and Warren, Waverly and Winthrop Streets, developed between about 1840 and 1920 and listed on the National Register on March 29, 1984.

areas.name: Frederick Douglass Square
areas.line: Lower Roxbury row houses in Second Empire, Queen Anne and Gothic styles, built on filled salt marsh between Hammond, Cabot, Windsor and Westminster Streets; the district was listed on the National Register on October 3, 1996.

rail.line: Commuter rail (Providence/Stoughton, Franklin/Foxboro and Needham Lines)
Silver Line SL4 and SL5 (bus rapid transit)

commute.text: The Silver Line runs on Washington Street from Nubian station, the SL4 to South Station and the SL5 to Downtown Crossing, following the route of the elevated line that closed in 1987. The Orange Line stops at Ruggles, on Tremont Street, and at Roxbury Crossing, at Tremont Street and Columbus Avenue, on the neighborhood's western side; Ruggles is also a stop on the Providence/Stoughton, Franklin/Foxboro and Needham commuter rail lines, though some trains pass it. Washington Street, Blue Hill Avenue, Columbus Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard are the main roads.

places.name: Franklin Park
places.line: Olmsted's park of roughly 485 acres, designed in the 1890s and Boston's largest open space, with the Franklin Park Zoo, the William Devine Golf Course and White Stadium; it connects Roxbury with Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan and Roslindale.

places.name: Franklin Park Zoo
places.line: A 72-acre zoo in the northeast part of Franklin Park, opened on October 4, 1912 and run by Zoo New England, with a 3-acre Tropical Forest building under a fabric dome.

places.name: Roxbury Heritage State Park
places.line: A state park at 183 Roxbury Street in John Eliot Square, built around the Dillaway-Thomas House of about 1750, now a museum, with landscaped grounds looking toward the Boston skyline.

places.name: Shirley-Eustis House
places.line: Governor William Shirley's summer house at 33 Shirley Street, built between 1747 and 1751 and later owned by Governor William Eustis; a National Historic Landmark since October 9, 1960, open to the public since 1991.

places.name: Highland Park and the Cochituate Standpipe
places.line: The park on the summit of Fort Hill, landscaped by Frederick Law Olmsted, with a Victorian tower designed by Nathaniel J. Bradlee around the standpipe Roxbury built in 1869 for its water system.

places.name: First Church in Roxbury
places.line: The congregation's meetinghouse in John Eliot Square, described as Boston's oldest surviving wooden meeting house of the Federal period.

places.name: Malcolm X-Ella Little-Collins House
places.line: A house at 72 Dale Street, built on part of the former Abijah Seaver estate, designated a Boston Landmark in 1998 and surveyed by city archaeologists in 2016.

history.text: Roxbury was settled on September 28.
Boston annexed the city of Roxbury on January 5.
The Washington Street Elevated opened on June 10, running as far as Dudley Square.
The elevated line closed on April 30, and the Orange Line reopened on May 4 in the Southwest Corridor, with new stations at Ruggles and Roxbury Crossing.
On December 19 the Public Improvement Commission renamed Dudley Square as Nubian Square, following a November 5 advisory ballot question.

faq.a: After a non-binding advisory question on the November 5, 2019 ballot, the city's Public Improvement Commission approved the change on December 19, 2019, and the MBTA's bus station there is now Nubian station. communities.title: Mattapan
communities.excerpt: Mattapan is a neighborhood in southern Boston, part of the town of Dorchester when Boston annexed it in 1870, centered on Mattapan Square, where Blue Hill Avenue, River Street and Cummins Highway meet.

ot_record.name: Mattapan
headline: The trolley's last stop at Mattapan Square,
triple-deckers, a nature sanctuary and the Neponset trail.
ot_record.answer: Mattapan is a neighborhood in southern Boston, part of the town of Dorchester when Boston annexed it in 1870, centered on Mattapan Square, where Blue Hill Avenue, River Street and Cummins Highway meet. Its housing includes triple-deckers, two- and three-family houses, single-family houses and small apartment buildings, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 23,834 people there in 2020. The Mattapan Line trolley ends at Mattapan station, and the Fairmount Line stops at Morton Street and Blue Hill Avenue.
ot_record.meta: Mattapan, Boston: triple-deckers and two-family houses around Mattapan Square, with the Mattapan Line trolley, two Fairmount Line stops and the Neponset trail.

boundaries.text: Mattapan is in the south of Boston, centered on Mattapan Square at the meeting of Blue Hill Avenue, River Street and Cummins Highway. Harambee Park in Dorchester's Franklin Field lies beside it, and the Boston Nature Center and Forest Hills Cemetery, in the adjoining Forest Hills area, are sometimes counted as its green space.

overview: Mattapan takes its name from the Massachusett name for the Dorchester area, recorded as 'Matampan' in 1634. Paths that became Adams Street and River Street led to fishing weirs at Lower Mills, and Mattapan and Lower Mills were the main fords of the Neponset River. On December 1, 1847, the Dorchester and Milton Branch Railroad began service to a station at Upper Mills that was later renamed Mattapan, and on December 18, 1849, the Mattapan Library Association opened. Mattapan was part of Dorchester when Boston annexed that town in 1870, and it grew in the late 19th and early 20th centuries as railroads and streetcars brought downtown within reach. The present Mattapan station building opened on July 4, 1902, after Blue Hill Avenue was widened.

In 1929 the Milton branch railroad became the Mattapan Line, a trolley that opened from Ashmont to Milton on August 26 and on to Mattapan on December 21; it runs beside the Neponset River and still uses PCC streetcars built in 1945 and 1946. The housing around the square includes triple-deckers, two- and three-family houses and single-family houses, with apartment buildings on parts of River Street. Boston State Hospital, in Mattapan and Dorchester, expanded onto the former Austin Farm in 1887 and closed in 1979; part of the grounds became Mass Audubon's Boston Nature Center, and 40 acres were redeveloped as Olmsted Green, 497 homes built in phases over 18 years, whose last phase, The Preserve, was sold out by February 2026.

The Fairmount Line's Morton Street station, a stop originally called Forest Avenue, reopened in October 1987 and was rebuilt to be accessible in 2007, and a new station at Blue Hill Avenue and Woodhaven Street opened on February 25, 2019. In April 2023 The Loop at Mattapan Station opened on the station's former parking lot, with 135 rental apartments and ground-floor retail. The Boston Planning & Development Agency board adopted PLAN: Mattapan on May 11, 2023; residential zoning allowing two- and three-unit infill and accessory dwelling units followed on February 7, 2024, and on May 30, 2024 Mattapan Square became the first place in the city mapped with Squares + Streets zoning, which allows mixed-use buildings and multifamily housing.

housing.text: The Boston Planning Department describes Mattapan's housing mix as small apartment buildings, single-family homes, public housing and Boston's traditional triple-deckers; two- and three-family houses are also part of the stock, and there are apartment buildings on parts of River Street. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 9,214 occupied housing units in Mattapan, 40.4% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: Mattapan Square
areas.line: The commercial center where Blue Hill Avenue, River Street and Cummins Highway meet, with Mattapan station at River Street and Blue Hill Avenue, the end of the trolley line and of eight bus routes; it was the first area mapped with Squares + Streets zoning, in 2024.

areas.name: Blue Hill Avenue
areas.line: With Mattapan Square, the neighborhood's main commercial street, with the Mattapan Branch Library at number 1350 and the Fairmount Line's Blue Hill Avenue station at Woodhaven Street.

areas.name: Former Boston State Hospital grounds
areas.line: The old hospital campus, closed in 1979, now divided between the 67-acre Boston Nature Center on Walk Hill Street and Olmsted Green, a 40-acre development of 497 homes, 80% of them deed-restricted affordable and 28% for ownership.

areas.name: Morton Street
areas.line: The corridor around Morton Street station at 865 Morton Street, a Fairmount Line stop between Talbot Avenue and Blue Hill Avenue.

rail.line: Mattapan Line (trolley, part of the Red Line)

commute.text: The Mattapan Line trolley runs about 2.6 miles from Mattapan station along the Neponset River to Ashmont, where it meets the Red Line. The Fairmount Line stops at Morton Street and Blue Hill Avenue on its way between Readville and South Station, through Dorchester. Eight MBTA bus routes end at Mattapan station, and Blue Hill Avenue, River Street, Cummins Highway and Morton Street are the main roads.

places.name: Boston Nature Center and Wildlife Sanctuary
places.line: Mass Audubon's 67-acre sanctuary at 500 Walk Hill Street, with gardens, meadows, woods and wetlands; admission is free, and part of the land was once Boston State Hospital.

places.name: Neponset River Greenway
places.line: A trail of about nine miles through Readville, Hyde Park, Mattapan and Dorchester and into Milton; a 1.3-mile section opened in May 2017 between the Mattapan and Central Avenue trolley stations, linking Mattapan Square to the trail toward Pope John Paul II Park.

places.name: Franklin Park
places.line: Olmsted's park of roughly 485 acres, designed in the 1890s and Boston's largest open space, with the Franklin Park Zoo, the William Devine Golf Course and White Stadium; it connects Mattapan with Roxbury, Dorchester, Jamaica Plain and Roslindale.

places.name: Harambee Park
places.line: A park built in 1898 to a Frederick Law Olmsted design and originally called Franklin Field, in Dorchester beside Mattapan.

places.name: Mattahunt Woods
places.line: A city Urban Wild with an entrance at 206 Colorado Street, where Boston Parks and Recreation, the Trustees and the Friends of Mattahunt Woods hold public programs.

places.name: Mattapan Branch Library
places.line: A Boston Public Library branch at 1350 Blue Hill Avenue, opened in February 2009; its history goes back to the Mattapan Library Association of 1849.

history.text: The Dorchester and Milton Branch Railroad began service on December 1 to a station at Upper Mills, later renamed Mattapan.
Boston annexed the town of Dorchester, which included Mattapan.
The branch railroad was converted to the Mattapan Line trolley, which reached Mattapan on December 21.

Squares + Streets zoning was encoded on May 30 for Mattapan's mixed-use and commercial areas, making Mattapan Square the first place in the city mapped with it, following PLAN: Mattapan, adopted May 11, 2023.

faq.q: What is the Mattapan trolley?
faq.a: The Mattapan Line, opened in 1929 on a former branch railroad, is a streetcar line of about 2.6 miles with eight stations between Ashmont and Mattapan that follows the Neponset River and uses PCC streetcars built in 1945 and 1946. faq.q: What is Squares + Streets zoning in Mattapan Square?
faq.a: It is a set of Boston zoning districts, adopted in April 2024 as part of the city's Squares + Streets initiative to increase housing production near transit; each district allows mixed-use buildings and multifamily housing. Mattapan Square was the first place mapped with it, on May 30, 2024, following PLAN: Mattapan, which the Boston Planning & Development Agency board adopted on May 11, 2023.

Its housing includes triple-deckers, two- and three-family houses, single-family houses and small apartment buildings, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 23,834 people there in 2020. The Mattapan Line trolley ends at Mattapan station, and the Fairmount Line stops at Morton Street and Blue Hill Avenue.

communities.title: Dorchester
communities.excerpt: Dorchester is Boston's largest neighborhood, more than 6 square miles between South Boston and the Neponset River, founded as a separate town in 1630 and annexed to Boston in stages that ended in 1870.

ot_record.name: Dorchester
headline: Squares strung along the Red Line,
three-deckers between them, the Neponset at the edge.
ot_record.answer: Dorchester is Boston's largest neighborhood, more than 6 square miles between South Boston and the Neponset River, founded as a separate town in 1630 and annexed to Boston in stages that ended in 1870. Its housing mixes single-family, two-family and three-decker homes and condominiums, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 122,191 people there in 2020. Five Red Line stations, the Mattapan Line and Fairmount Line commuter rail stations including Uphams Corner, Four Corners/Geneva and Talbot Avenue serve it.
ot_record.meta: Dorchester, Boston: three-deckers and Victorian houses around Fields Corner, Savin Hill, Codman Square and Lower Mills, on the Red Line and Fairmount Line.

boundaries.text: Dorchester is bordered by South Boston, the South End, Roxbury, Jamaica Plain and Hyde Park; the Neponset River separates it from Quincy and Milton, and Dorchester Bay lies to the east. It is often divided into North Dorchester, the part north of Quincy, East and Freeport Streets, and South Dorchester.

overview: Settlers who came on the Mary and John landed at Columbia Point in June 1630 and founded Dorchester months before Boston. The town held what is described as the first town meeting in what became the United States on October 8, 1633, buried its dead in the North Burying Ground at today's Uphams Corner from 1634, and opened the Mather School in 1639. Israel Stoughton built a grist mill on the Neponset River in 1634, and from 1765 chocolate was refined at Lower Mills, where the Walter Baker company made it until 1965. Boston took Dorchester in pieces, starting with Dorchester Neck (now South Boston) in 1804, and annexed the rest of the town in 1870.

Dorchester grew as a streetcar suburb. The Old Colony Railroad crossed it from 1845, Dorchester Avenue carried a horse-drawn streetcar, and by 1890 the streetcar and the three-decker had come together here, with three-deckers filling the land between the old village centers. Those centers are still the neighborhood's commercial squares: Uphams Corner and Bowdoin/Geneva in the north; Fields Corner, Codman Square, Peabody Square at Ashmont, Adams Village and Lower Mills to the south. The Red Line's Dorchester stations opened in 1927 and 1928, from Columbia (now JFK/UMass) through Savin Hill, Fields Corner and Shawmut to Ashmont.

Columbia Point, where the first settlers landed, now holds UMass Boston, which moved there in 1974, the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library, dedicated in 1979, the Edward M. Kennedy Institute and the Massachusetts Archives. The Fairmount Line gained new Dorchester stations at Talbot Avenue in November 2012 and Four Corners/Geneva in July 2013, and Pope John Paul II Park opened in 2001 on a former drive-in and dump along the Neponset. In May 2024 the Boston Planning Department began a Squares + Streets plan for Fields Corner, part of a citywide program covering housing, public space, small businesses and transportation in neighborhood centers; the department's project page showed it still in progress, with no adoption date.

housing.text: Dorchester's housing includes single-family, two-family and three-family houses and condominiums. Three-decker apartment buildings went up in large numbers alongside the streetcar lines from around 1890, and Victorian houses fill hills such as Savin Hill, where lots were sold after the Civil War. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 44,979 occupied housing units, 37.3% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: Savin Hill
areas.line: A hill above Dorchester Bay, first called Rock Hill and renamed in 1819, built up with Victorian houses after the Civil War; it has a Red Line station from 1927 and Savin Hill and Malibu beaches nearby.

areas.name: Fields Corner
areas.line: A commercial district centered on the X-shaped crossing of Dorchester Avenue and Adams Street, named for Zechariah Field, with the 1874 Fields Corner Municipal Building and a Red Line station; side streets hold three-deckers and Victorian houses.

areas.name: Ashmont
areas.line: The area around Ashmont station at Dorchester Avenue and Ashmont Street, the Red Line's southern terminus on this branch and the transfer point to the Mattapan Line, with Peabody Square's shops beside it.

areas.name: Lower Mills
areas.line: The old mill village on the Neponset River at the Milton line, where the Walter Baker chocolate buildings, a major part of them built from 1868, now hold mixed industrial, retail and residential uses; the district was listed on the National Register in 1980.

areas.name: Uphams Corner
areas.line: The square where Columbia Road meets Dudley and Stoughton Streets, named for grocer Amos Upham, with the 1918 Strand Theatre, the 1634 North Burying Ground and a Fairmount Line station.

areas.name: Codman Square
areas.line: The crossing of Washington Street and Talbot Avenue, a National Register district since 1983 that includes the 1806 Second Church in Dorchester and the 1904 Codman Square branch library; Talbot Avenue station on the Fairmount Line is nearby.

commute.text: The Red Line's Ashmont branch has five stations in Dorchester, and at Ashmont it meets the Mattapan Line trolley, which stops at Cedar Grove in southern Dorchester. The Fairmount Line runs from South Station through Newmarket, Uphams Corner, Four Corners/Geneva and Talbot Avenue toward Readville. I-93, Route 203 and Route 28 (Blue Hill Avenue) cross the neighborhood, along with Gallivan Boulevard and Morton Street.

places.name: John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum
places.line: I. M. Pei's library on a 9.5-acre site at the tip of Columbia Point, beside UMass Boston, dedicated on October 20, 1979, with a glass and steel pavilion 115 feet high.

places.name: James Blake House
places.line: Built in 1661, a date confirmed by tree-ring dating in 2007, and described as the oldest surviving house in Boston; it stands at 735 Columbia Road in Edward Everett Square and is owned by the Dorchester Historical Society.

places.name: Pope John Paul II Park
places.line: A 66-acre DCR park on the Neponset River, opened in 2001 on the site of the Neponset Drive-In and the Hallet Street dump, with trails including the Lower Neponset River Trail.

places.name: Franklin Park
places.line: Olmsted's 485-acre park, Boston's largest open space, which connects Dorchester with Roxbury, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan and Roslindale; it holds the Franklin Park Zoo and the William Devine Golf Course.

places.name: Strand Theatre
places.line: A theater at Uphams Corner, opened in 1918 as one of the first built specifically for motion pictures.

places.name: Dorchester North Burying Ground
places.line: A burying ground at Uphams Corner dating to 1634, one of the oldest in the country.

places.name: Dorchester-Milton Lower Mills Industrial District
places.line: The Walter Baker chocolate complex on both banks of the Neponset, where chocolate was made from 1765 until 1965, now in mixed industrial, retail and residential use.

history.text: Settlers from the Mary and John landed at Columbia Point on June 17 and founded the town of Dorchester.
Dorchester held what is described as the first town meeting in what became the United States, on October 8.
Dr. James Baker and John Hannan began making chocolate at Lower Mills, the start of the Walter Baker company.
After a June 1869 vote, the rest of the town of Dorchester was annexed to Boston.

faq.q: Does Dorchester have commuter rail?
faq.a: Yes. The Fairmount Line stops at Uphams Corner, Four Corners/Geneva and Talbot Avenue in Dorchester on its way between South Station and Readville. The Red Line also has five Dorchester stations, from JFK/UMass to Ashmont.

faq.q: What are Dorchester's main squares?
faq.a: Dorchester's commercial districts grew from its old village centers: Uphams Corner and Bowdoin/Geneva in the north, and Fields Corner, Codman Square, Peabody Square at Ashmont, Adams Village and Lower Mills in the south. Residential sections include Savin Hill, Jones Hill, Meeting House Hill, Ashmont Hill, Neponset, Port Norfolk, Popes Hill and Cedar Grove.

communities.title: South Boston
communities.excerpt: South Boston is a Boston neighborhood on the former Dorchester Neck, south and east of Fort Point Channel along Dorchester Bay, annexed to Boston in 1804.

ot_record.name: South Boston
headline: Dorchester Heights at the center,
Castle Island and three miles of beach and parkland at the end of Broadway.
ot_record.answer: South Boston is a Boston neighborhood on the former Dorchester Neck, south and east of Fort Point Channel along Dorchester Bay, annexed to Boston in 1804. Its housing includes 19th-century brick and mansard row houses and flat-roofed triple-deckers, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 37,917 people there in 2020, with the South Boston Waterfront counted separately. The Red Line stops at Broadway and Andrew, and Castle Island anchors three miles of shoreline parks.
ot_record.meta: South Boston: row houses and triple-deckers from Dorchester Heights to Castle Island, with Red Line stops at Broadway and Andrew and three miles of shoreline parks.

boundaries.text: South Boston lies south and east of Fort Point Channel, along Dorchester Bay, with Castle Island beside City Point and Andrew station on its west side. The Seaport, or South Boston Waterfront, north of the residential streets is treated by the city's planners as a separate neighborhood.

overview: South Boston was Dorchester Neck, a narrow peninsula belonging to the town of Dorchester. On the night of March 4, 1776, Continental troops fortified Dorchester Heights, and the British evacuated Boston on March 17. Boston annexed the peninsula in 1804, bridges over Fort Point Channel tied it to downtown, and landfill widened its connection to the mainland. In 1822 land on the peninsula was set aside for public institutions, including a jail and an almshouse; after they moved, East Broadway was extended to the end of the peninsula in 1854 and 4.5 acres became Independence Square.

The streets climb to Dorchester Heights, the highest area of South Boston. Near the top of Telegraph Hill, an 1849 reservoir was later filled and replaced by South Boston High School in 1901, and the rest of the summit was laid out in the 1850s as Thomas Park, now centered on a 115-foot marble monument completed in 1902. Mansard and brick row houses, some with marble and sandstone fronts, went up around Independence Square in the fifteen years after the Civil War. At City Point the granite Fort Independence, built between 1833 and 1848, stands on Castle Island, which the city joined to the mainland by filling the flats between 1890 and the 1920s; Day Boulevard now runs past Pleasure Bay, M Street Beach and Carson Beach.

Recent city planning has looked at the neighborhood's edges. The Boston Planning & Development Agency completed PLAN: South Boston Dorchester Avenue in December 2016, with the projects reviewed under it mostly on Dorchester Avenue, Old Colony Avenue and nearby streets, and a follow-up transportation plan was finalized in 2021. To the north, the waterfront along Fort Point Channel and Boston Harbor was the focus of the city's 1,000-acre Innovation District plan announced in 2010, and the city's research tables report it as the separate South Boston Waterfront neighborhood.

housing.text: South Boston's housing includes mansard and brick row houses from the 1860s and 1870s around Independence Square and along East Broadway, and triple-deckers, which here were mostly built with flat roofs. The Boston Housing Authority's Mary Ellen McCormack (1936) and Old Colony (1941) developments are in the neighborhood, and the second phase of Old Colony's redevelopment was completed in 2014. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 17,109 occupied housing units, 43.4% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: City Point
areas.line: The eastern end of the peninsula near Castle Island, reached by East Broadway and Day Boulevard, where MBTA bus routes 7, 9, 10 and 11 end at the City Point bus terminal.

areas.name: Independence Square
areas.line: A 4.5-acre square on East Broadway laid out in 1854, ringed by mansard and brick row houses built mostly in the fifteen years after the Civil War, including the Harrison Loring House at 789 East Broadway, the first house on the square.

areas.name: Dorchester Heights and Telegraph Hill
areas.line: The highest area of South Boston, with Thomas Park and the Dorchester Heights Monument on the summit of Telegraph Hill and South Boston High School on the site of an 1849 reservoir; a 40-acre area centered on Thomas Park was listed on the National Register as the Dorchester Heights Historic District in 2001.

areas.name: West Broadway and Andrew Square
areas.line: The western side along Broadway and Dorchester Avenue, served by the Broadway and Andrew Red Line stations; Andrew Square is where Dorchester Avenue, Dorchester Street, Southampton Street and Boston Street meet.

commute.text: The Red Line's Broadway station, at Dorchester Avenue and Broadway, opened in 1917, and Andrew station, at Andrew Square, in 1918; both run north to South Station, where the Fairmount, Needham, Providence/Stoughton and other south-side commuter rail lines end. MBTA bus routes 7, 9, 10 and 11 cross the neighborhood to the City Point terminal, and Andrew connects with routes including the 10, 16, 17, 18 and 171. The Silver Line serves the separate Waterfront area, and the Big Dig put I-93 below ground.

places.name: Castle Island and Fort Independence
places.line: A DCR park at 2010 Day Boulevard, where the Castle Island Loop circles the granite Fort Independence, built from 1833 and listed on the National Register in 1970; open sunrise to sunset.

places.name: Pleasure Bay, M Street Beach and Carson Beach
places.line: Part of a three-mile stretch of beach and parkland along Day Boulevard, with an accessible loop around Pleasure Bay; dogs are not allowed on the beach from May 1 through September 15.

places.name: Dorchester Heights Monument
places.line: A white marble Georgian Revival tower by Peabody and Stearns, completed in 1902 to mark the fortification of March 4, 1776, and stewarded by the National Park Service as part of Boston National Historical Park.

places.name: Thomas Park
places.line: A roughly elliptical park of walks and ornamental plantings laid out in the 1850s on the summit of Telegraph Hill on Dorchester Heights, centered on the monument.

places.name: Independence Square
places.line: A 4.5-acre park created in 1854 on East Broadway, which received 150 trees and granite steps in 1874.

places.name: Saint Augustine Chapel
places.line: A chapel completed in 1819 and described as the oldest Catholic church in Massachusetts.

history.text: Continental troops fortified Dorchester Heights on March 4, and the British evacuated Boston on March 17.
Boston annexed South Boston, part of the town of Dorchester's Dorchester Neck.
Work began on the present granite Fort Independence on Castle Island, substantially complete by 1848.
Broadway station opened on December 15 as part of the Red Line's Dorchester Extension; Andrew followed in 1918.
