communities.title: Allston
communities.excerpt: Allston is a Boston neighborhood on the Charles River, the eastern part of the former town of Brighton, named in 1868 when its railroad station and post office took the name of the painter Washington Allston; it became part of Boston with Brighton in 1874.

ot_record.name: Allston
headline: Brick apartments on Commonwealth Avenue,
former rail yards and Harvard's Lower Allston campus on the Charles.
ot_record.answer: Allston is a Boston neighborhood on the Charles River, the eastern part of the former town of Brighton, named in 1868 when its railroad station and post office took the name of the painter Washington Allston; it became part of Boston with Brighton in 1874. It had 24,904 residents in the 2020 Census, as tabulated by the Boston Planning Department. Its housing runs from brick apartment buildings on Commonwealth Avenue to triple-deckers and Victorian houses, and the Green Line B branch runs along Commonwealth Avenue.
ot_record.meta: Allston, Boston: brick apartments, triple-deckers and Victorian houses on the Charles, by Harvard Stadium, with the Green Line B branch and the I-90 project.

boundaries.text: The Charles River forms Allston's northern and eastern edges, across from Cambridge; it borders Brighton, generally along Everett, Gordon and Kelton Streets, as well as the Fenway-Kenmore area and the town of Brookline. The Massachusetts Turnpike crosses it, with Lower (North) Allston north of Cambridge Street and the Turnpike.

overview: Allston grew up as the eastern part of Little Cambridge, which became the town of Brighton in 1807. The Boston and Albany Railroad opened a new depot here in 1867, and in 1868 the station and post office in Brighton's eastern portion took the name Allston, after the painter Washington Allston. Allston became part of Boston when Brighton was annexed in 1874, and it has never been a separate municipality. Railroad and livestock operations shaped the area; the livestock trade ended by the mid-20th century, and the Beacon Park rail yard, later CSX's Beacon Park Yard, stayed in use until 2013. Streetcar service along Commonwealth Avenue began on May 18, 1896, from Governors Square to Brighton Avenue.

Large institutions arrived in the 20th century. Harvard Stadium, an early large structure in reinforced concrete, opened on November 14, 1903, and was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1987. Harvard Business School, founded in 1908, has its campus in Lower Allston; its Morgan Hall dates from 1927. Braves Field opened on August 18, 1915, at Commonwealth Avenue and Babcock Street on the site of the Allston Golf Club, and Boston University bought it on July 30, 1953; Boston University's schools and facilities now extend from Kenmore Square to Packard's Corner. The Massachusetts Turnpike Extension opened through Allston in 1964 and 1965, largely on the old Boston and Albany right-of-way. The Boston Planning Department counts 358 acres of academic space in Allston, the most of any Boston neighborhood, and notes that Harvard owns more land in Boston than in Cambridge.

Brick apartment buildings line Commonwealth Avenue and nearby streets, wooden triple-deckers stand along Brighton Avenue toward Brighton, and Lower Allston has Victorian single- and multi-family houses built between the 1890s and 1920s. Harvard's Science and Engineering Complex opened in 2020. In 2019 work began on a bus lane from Union Square to Packard's Corner. The largest pending change is MassDOT's I-90 Allston Multimodal Project, which is progressing the design to replace the I-90 viaduct in Allston; MassDOT says cost and engineering analyses by an independent review team are to be examined in 2026. The plans include West Station, proposed at Ashford Street in the former Beacon Park Yard on the Framingham/Worcester Line.

housing.text: Allston's housing is mostly brick apartment buildings, especially on Commonwealth Avenue and nearby streets, with wooden triple-deckers along Brighton Avenue and Victorian single- and multi-family houses from the 1890s to the 1920s in Lower Allston. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 8,040 occupied housing units in Allston, 14.0% of them owner-occupied and 86.0% renter-occupied, compared with 35.3% owner-occupied citywide.

areas.name: Lower Allston (North Allston)
areas.line: The section north of Cambridge Street and the Turnpike, from Everett Street east to the Charles River, centered on Allston Square at Western Avenue and North Harvard Street; Harvard Business School and most of Harvard's athletic facilities are here.

areas.name: Union Square
areas.line: Home to the Allston fire station (Engine 41 and Ladder 14), and the start of a bus lane to Packard's Corner built from 2019.

areas.name: Harvard Avenue and Allston Village
areas.line: The commercial blocks between Commonwealth Avenue and Cambridge Street, with shops and restaurants and a Green Line stop at Harvard Avenue.

areas.name: Packard's Corner
areas.line: Named after Packard's Sales Stable and Riding School, with a Green Line stop; Boston University's schools and facilities extend from Kenmore Square to here.

commute.text: The Green Line B branch runs along Commonwealth Avenue, with stops from Babcock Street to Allston Street, toward Kenmore and downtown. MBTA bus route 57 follows the path of the former A branch along Brighton Avenue, and routes 64, 66, 70 and 86 also serve Allston. Allston has no commuter rail station today; Boston Landing station in Brighton is on the Framingham/Worcester Line, and West Station is proposed in the former Beacon Park Yard. The Massachusetts Turnpike crosses the neighborhood, and the Paul Dudley White Bicycle Path follows the Charles River along its northern and eastern edges.

places.name: Harvard Stadium
places.line: Opened on November 14, 1903, on North Harvard Street, a pioneering large structure in reinforced concrete that seats just over 25,000; a National Historic Landmark since 1987.

places.name: Harvard Business School
places.line: Founded in 1908, with its campus in Lower Allston; Morgan Hall (1927) and Loeb House (1940) were designed by McKim, Mead & White.

places.name: Harvard Science and Engineering Complex
places.line: Home to Harvard's John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, opened in 2020 next to Harvard Business School and the Harvard Innovation Labs.

places.name: Nickerson Field
places.line: Boston University's field at 285 Babcock Street, on the site of Braves Field, the Boston Braves' ballpark from 1915 to 1952; the entry gate, right field pavilion and old ticket office survive.

places.name: Ringer Park
places.line: A city park established in 1916, with a Little League field, tennis and basketball courts, a playground, walking paths and a wooded area with trails; design work on its renovation was paused in September 2023 while the city sought grants.

places.name: Charles River and the Paul Dudley White Bicycle Path
places.line: The river and the Paul Dudley White Bicycle Path border Allston to the north and east, used for canoeing, running and biking.

history.text: The railroad station and post office in eastern Brighton took the name Allston, after the painter Washington Allston.
Allston became part of Boston when the town of Brighton was annexed on January 5.
Harvard Stadium opened on November 14.
The Massachusetts Turnpike Extension opened through Allston in 1964 and 1965, largely on the former Boston and Albany Railroad right-of-way.

ot_record.answer: Brighton is a neighborhood in the northwestern corner of Boston, incorporated as its own town in 1807 and annexed to Boston in 1874, with 52,047 residents in 2020 (2020 Census, Boston Planning Department tabulation). boundaries.text: The northwestern corner of Boston: the Charles River separates it from Cambridge and Watertown, Newton lies to the west and Brookline to the south, and it meets Allston generally along Everett, Gordon and Kelton Streets.

overview: The land that became Brighton was assigned to Watertown in 1630 and moved to Newtowne, later Cambridge, in 1634; the settlement south of the Charles was known as Little Cambridge. In 1775 Jonathan Winship I and Jonathan Winship II established a cattle market here to supply the Continental Army. After disputes with Cambridge over the cattle trade and the failure to repair the Great Bridge, Little Cambridge was incorporated as the town of Brighton on February 24, 1807. The Boston & Worcester Railroad came through in 1834, and by 1866 the town had 41 slaughterhouses, later consolidated into the Brighton Stock Yards and the Brighton Abattoir. Brighton, then in Middlesex County, voted in October 1873 to join Boston, and annexation took effect on January 5, 1874.

The old town center runs along Washington Street. The Brighton Center Historic District, 15 acres around the junction of Washington Street with Market Street and Chestnut Hill Avenue, was listed on the National Register on February 20, 2001; its oldest resource is the Market Street Burial Ground of 1764. In the southwest corner, the Chestnut Hill Reservoir was dedicated on October 25, 1870, as part of Boston's water supply. Nearby, the Aberdeen section was developed after 1887 as a suburb of detached houses along winding roads, served by the Beacon Street trolley, in Colonial Revival, Georgian Revival, Queen Anne and Shingle styles. Brighton is also home to Saint John's Seminary, whose classes began in 1884, portions of Boston College, and St. Elizabeth's Medical Center, founded in 1868.

The Boston Planning Department describes Brighton's housing as wooden triple-deckers, suburban-style single-family houses and brick apartment buildings, with business districts in Brighton Center, Cleveland Circle and Oak Square. Since the mid-2010s, New Balance has developed Boston Landing, a mixed-use district around Guest Street: it built its headquarters on Guest Street in 2015, the Warrior Ice Arena opened on September 8, 2016, and Boston Landing station opened on May 22, 2017, with New Balance funding its design, construction and maintenance. WGBH built its headquarters on Guest Street in 2007. On the river, the Charles River Speedway headquarters at 525 Western Avenue, built between 1899 and 1940, was rehabilitated from 2019 and reopened as The Speedway in 2021.

housing.text: Brighton's housing includes wooden triple-deckers, suburban-style single-family houses and brick apartment buildings, according to the Boston Planning Department; the Aberdeen section holds detached houses in Colonial Revival, Georgian Revival, Queen Anne and Shingle styles, along with apartment and condominium buildings. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 21,002 occupied housing units in Brighton, 22.7% of them owner-occupied and 77.3% renter-occupied, compared with 35.3% owner-occupied citywide.

areas.name: Brighton Center

areas.name: Boston Landing

commute.text: The Green Line B branch runs along Commonwealth Avenue to its terminus at Boston College, the C branch ends at Cleveland Circle, and the D branch's Reservoir station is one block south of Brighton. Boston Landing station, at Everett and Guest Streets, is on the Framingham/Worcester commuter rail line. MBTA bus routes 57, 64, 65, 66, 70, 86 and 501 serve the neighborhood. The Massachusetts Turnpike passes through northern Brighton, and Soldiers Field Road follows the Charles toward Storrow Drive and downtown.

places.name: The Speedway

places.line: A hockey arena and Boston Bruins practice rink at 90 Guest Street in Boston Landing, built by New Balance and opened on September 8, 2016.

places.line: The archdiocesan seminary, whose first classes began on September 22, 1884; after land sales in the 2000s, nearly all of them to Boston College (which bought the main property in June 2004), its campus consists only of Saint John's Hall.

places.name: St. Elizabeth's Medical Center
places.line: A teaching hospital founded in 1868, operated by Boston Medical Center Health System since October 1, 2024.

ot_record.name: Cambridge
headline: Newtowne of 1630 on the Charles,
five Red Line stops and a reservoir to the west.
ot_record.answer: Cambridge is a Middlesex County city of 118,403 people (2020 Census) on the north bank of the Charles River, across from Boston. Single-family homes are a small share of its housing: 6.4% of units, against 34.1% in buildings of more than 100 units, by the city's own count. The Warren Group recorded 105 single-family sales in 2025, a small market for a city of this size. Five Red Line stations run through Cambridge, from Alewife to Kendall/MIT, and Porter also has commuter rail.
overview: Cambridge was founded in December 1630 as Newtowne and renamed in May 1638 after the English university town, two years after the college that became Harvard was founded. George Washington took command of the Continental Army on Cambridge Common in 1775 and used the house at 105 Brattle Street as his first long-term headquarters during the siege of Boston. The West Boston Bridge of 1792 tied the town directly to Boston, and new bridges and roads turned estates and marshland into industrial and residential districts; the New England Glass Company, founded in 1818, with plants in what are now Kendall Square and East Cambridge, was the city's largest employer for much of the 19th century. Cambridge became a city in 1846. MIT moved here from Boston in 1916.

The city recognizes 13 neighborhoods on about 6.4 square miles of land. Squares strung along Massachusetts Avenue anchor them: Harvard Square beside the 22.4-acre Harvard Yard, where Massachusetts Hall has stood since 1720, Central Square with City Hall, and Porter Square farther north, while Kendall Square grew from salt marsh and 19th-century industry into an office and laboratory district beside MIT. Cambridgeport keeps streets of triple-deckers near the river. In the west, Fresh Pond Reservation surrounds the city's drinking-water reservoir, and Mount Auburn Cemetery, founded in 1831, straddles the line with Watertown. Danehy Park, a 50-acre former city dump in North Cambridge, opened as parkland in 1990.

On February 10, 2025, the City Council voted to allow multifamily housing citywide. Multifamily housing is now allowed in every zoning district except Open Space, and in the new base district, Residence C-1, residential buildings may rise to four stories (45 feet), or to six stories (74 feet) on lots of at least 5,000 square feet when 20 percent of the housing is income-restricted. Existing single-family homes may remain and new ones may still be built, and the city's inclusionary housing program continues. Since October 2020, the 100 Percent Affordable Housing Overlay, amended in 2023 and 2025, has allowed permanently affordable buildings denser than base zoning; completed projects include 52 New Street (106 rental units) and 116 Norfolk Street (62). The state lists Cambridge as compliant with the MBTA Communities law.

housing.text: By the city's inventory as of June 30, 2025, 6.4% of Cambridge's housing units are single-family homes, 11.9% are in two-unit buildings and 10.5% in three-unit buildings, while 34.1% are in buildings of more than 100 units. About two-thirds of occupied units (66.5%) are renter-occupied and 33.5% owner-occupied (2020 to 2024 American Community Survey). With so few single-family homes, The Warren Group's 105 single-family sales in 2025 reflect only a narrow part of the market.

villages.name: Harvard Square
villages.line: A triangular plaza where Massachusetts Avenue, Brattle Street and John F. Kennedy Street meet beside Harvard Yard, served by Harvard station on the Red Line and a bus hub.

villages.name: Central Square
villages.line: The seat of city government, centered where Massachusetts Avenue, Prospect Street and Western Avenue meet; a state-designated Cultural District since 2012, with Central station on the Red Line.

villages.name: Kendall Square
villages.line: Former Charles River salt marsh and industrial district where Main Street meets Broadway, named for the Kendall Boiler and Tank Company, now an office and lab district beside MIT with the Kendall/MIT Red Line stop.

villages.name: Cambridgeport
villages.line: A mostly residential neighborhood of triple-deckers between Massachusetts Avenue and the Charles River, with Magazine Beach and Fort Washington Park.

villages.name: East Cambridge
villages.line: The old Lechmere Point, once home to glassworks and factory cottages, between the Charles River, Somerville and Broadway, with Lechmere station relocated in 2022 for the Green Line Extension.

villages.name: Porter Square
villages.line: The square where Massachusetts Avenue meets Somerville Avenue, spanning Cambridge and Somerville, renamed in 1896 for Porter's Hotel and once lined with cattle yards; the Red Line reached Porter station in 1984, and it is also a Fitchburg Line commuter rail stop.

commute.text: Five Red Line stations serve Cambridge, from Alewife, which has a 2,471-space MBTA garage, through Porter, Harvard and Central to Kendall/MIT. Porter is also a Fitchburg Line commuter rail stop, about 15 minutes from Boston's North Station, and Lechmere in East Cambridge is on the Green Line. Route 2 enters at Alewife and runs with US 3 and Route 16 along Alewife Brook and Fresh Pond Parkways, then with US 3 along Memorial Drive beside the Charles.

places.name: Fresh Pond Reservation
places.line: 162 acres of open space around the 155-acre Fresh Pond reservoir, part of the city's drinking-water system, with nature walks and ranger programs.

places.name: Mount Auburn Cemetery
places.line: Established in 1831 between Cambridge and Watertown, a National Historic Landmark open to the public at no cost every day of the year.

places.name: Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters
places.line: A National Historic Site at 105 Brattle Street, Washington's headquarters during the siege of Boston and later Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's home, with seasonal tours and a formal garden.

places.name: Cambridge Common
places.line: Public parkland where Washington took command of the Continental Army in 1775.

places.name: Harvard Yard
places.line: A 22.4-acre grassy enclosure bounded principally by Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge Street, Broadway and Quincy Street, with Massachusetts Hall (1720), Harvard's oldest building, and Widener Library.

places.name: Danehy Park
places.line: A 50-acre North Cambridge park on a former brickyard and city dump, opened in 1990, with athletic fields, paths, a wetland area and the city's first Miyawaki forest, planted in 2021; the eastern entrance is at 99 Sherman Street.

places.name: MIT Museum
places.line: MIT's museum, founded in 1971, reopened on October 2, 2022 in the Gambrill Center at 314 Main Street in Kendall Square, beside the Kendall/MIT station; its collections include holography, robotics, architecture and the history of MIT.

places.name: Cambridge Public Library
places.line: The main library at 449 Broadway joins a Richardsonian Romanesque building of 1888 by Van Brunt & Howe with an expansion that opened on November 8, 2009; six neighborhood branches serve the rest of the city.

The college that became Harvard was founded.
George Washington took command of the Patriot soldiers on Cambridge Common.
Cambridge was incorporated as a city.

ot_record.name: Somerville
headline: A powder house, a hilltop castle,
and five Green Line stops opened in 2022.
ot_record.meta: Somerville is a Middlesex County city of 81,045 people (2020 Census) just north of Cambridge and Boston. Triple-deckers, transit and 2025 prices, sourced.
ot_record.answer: Somerville is a Middlesex County city of 81,045 people (2020 Census) on about 4.1 square miles of land just north of Cambridge and Boston, often described as the most densely populated municipality in New England. It is known for its triple-deckers, and since November 2023 three-unit buildings have been allowed citywide by right. The Warren Group counted only 72 single-family sales in 2025. Davis Square is on the Red Line, Assembly on the Orange Line, and five Green Line stations opened in 2022.
overview: Somerville was settled in 1629 as part of Charlestown and became its own town in 1842 and a city in 1872. Its hills played a part in the Revolution: British troops emptied the Old Powder House of gunpowder on September 1, 1774, setting off the Powder Alarm, and Prospect Hill was a Continental Army position during the siege of Boston, where tradition says Washington raised a flag on January 1, 1776. The Boston and Lowell Railroad opened in the 1840s, and in 1843 George O. Brastow laid out one of Somerville's first residential subdivisions on the south side of Spring Hill. Brickmaking, meatpacking and a Ford assembly plant, open from 1926 to 1958, followed.

The city is organized around its squares. Davis Square, a six-point intersection named for grain dealer Person Davis, gained a Red Line station in 1984, and the Somerville Community Path runs from there on an old railroad right-of-way. Union Square, named for its Civil War recruiting role, and Ball Square have Green Line stations that opened in 2022, and Assembly Square on the Mystic River grew from the old Ford plant site into the Assembly Row development. On Spring Hill, most buildings are wood-frame Greek Revival and Victorian houses of one to three units, with triple-deckers filling the remaining land in the early 1900s. The 2020 Census counted 36,269 housing units in the city.

Somerville adopted an entirely new zoning ordinance on December 12, 2019, its first major overhaul since 1990. The code sets standards for 23 building types, allows backyard cottages, requires most new developments to make 20 percent of their units affordable, and removed minimum parking requirements for most of the city, with maximums near Red, Orange and Green Line stations. In November 2023 the City Council made three-unit buildings legal by right citywide. The state housing office (EOHLC) approved Somerville's multifamily zoning ordinance on October 1, 2024, and the state lists the city as compliant with the MBTA Communities law. The city has since opened a five-year review of the 2019 code.

housing.text: Somerville is known for its triple-deckers. In November 2023 the City Council made any three-unit building legal citywide by right, without zoning board approval, replacing 2019 rules that required a new triple-decker to sit next to an existing one and include an income-restricted unit. Single-family homes are a small part of the market: The Warren Group counted 72 single-family sales in 2025.

villages.name: Davis Square
villages.line: A six-point intersection in northwestern Somerville, named a square in 1883, with the 1914 Somerville Theatre and a Red Line station opened in December 1984.

villages.name: Union Square
villages.line: The southeastern square at Washington Street, Webster Avenue and Somerville Avenue, once called Sand Pit Square, with Prospect Hill nearby and a Green Line station opened March 21, 2022.

villages.name: Ball Square
villages.line: A square on the Somerville-Medford line with a Green Line Extension station opened December 12, 2022.

villages.name: Assembly Square
villages.line: Named for a Ford assembly plant that ran from 1926 to 1958, on the west bank of the Mystic River between I-93 and the river, now the 45-acre Assembly Row development with an Orange Line station.

villages.name: Spring Hill
villages.line: A drumlin ridge in central Somerville roughly between Highland Avenue, Somerville Avenue, Elm Street and Willow Avenue, with Summer Street along its crest and the Spring Hill Historic District, listed on the National Register in 1989.

villages.name: Winter Hill
villages.line: The hill roughly north of Medford Street, with Foss Park at its base beside I-93, a Revolutionary War fort site, restored houses and triple-deckers, and Green Line stations at Gilman Square and Magoun Square.

rail.line: Green Line (subway, Union Square and Medford branches)
Fitchburg Line (commuter rail, in neighboring Cambridge)

commute.text: Somerville has no commuter rail station of its own; passenger rail service in the city ended by 1958, and the nearest stop is Porter in Cambridge on the Fitchburg Line. Rapid transit has returned in stages: Davis on the Red Line in 1984, Assembly on the Orange Line, and the Green Line Extension in 2022, with Union Square on one branch and East Somerville, Gilman Square, Magoun Square and Ball Square on the branch to Medford/Tufts. I-93 crosses the city on an elevated highway, Route 28 runs as McGrath Highway and Route 38 as Mystic Avenue.

places.name: Old Powder House
places.line: Built as a windmill around 1703 or 1704 and later a powder magazine, it overlooks Powder House Square from Nathan Tufts Park; both were listed on the National Register in 1975.

places.name: Prospect Hill Monument
places.line: A castle-like tower dedicated in 1903 atop Prospect Hill, a Continental Army position during the siege of Boston.

places.name: Somerville Community Path
places.line: A walking and biking path on a former Boston and Maine right-of-way from Davis Square, extended 1.9 miles beside the Green Line to North Point in Cambridge in June 2023.

places.name: Somerville Theatre
places.line: A Davis Square theater opened in 1914 that shows films and live performances.

places.name: Assembly Row
places.line: A 45-acre mixed-use development on the Mystic River, opened in 2014, with shops, restaurants, a 12-screen cinema and a hotel.

places.name: Mystic River Reservation (Draw Seven Park)
places.line: A DCR reservation of 329 acres along the Mystic River in Winchester, Arlington, Medford, Somerville, Everett and Chelsea, with field sports, picnicking, cycling and sailing at four riverside parks; Draw Seven Park is in Somerville, and its reconstruction was expected to last from late summer 2024 to 2026.

places.name: Somerville Museum
places.line: Run by the Somerville Historical Society in a 1920s Federal Revival building at One Westwood Road, at Central Street, with exhibits of local and historical significance and music and lecture series.

history.text: First European settlement, as part of Charlestown.
British regulars removed gunpowder from the Old Powder House on September 1, setting off the Powder Alarm.
Somerville separated from Charlestown and was incorporated as a town.
Somerville was incorporated as a city.
The Green Line Extension opened Union Square station on March 21 and the Medford branch, with East Somerville, Gilman Square, Magoun Square and Ball Square stations, on December 12.

faq.q: What are Somerville's zoning rules for new housing?
faq.a: Somerville adopted a new zoning ordinance on December 12, 2019, which requires most new developments to make 20 percent of their units affordable and removed minimum parking requirements for most of the city. communities.excerpt: Plymouth is a Plymouth County town of 61,217 people (2020 Census) on Cape Cod Bay, about 40 miles south of Boston, and the largest municipality in Massachusetts by area.

ot_record.name: Plymouth
headline: A harbor town of 1620,
with pine forest and ponds filling its western miles.
ot_record.meta: Plymouth is a Plymouth County town of 61,217 people (2020 Census) on Cape Cod Bay, about 40 miles south of Boston. Homes, transit and 2025 prices, sourced.
ot_record.answer: Plymouth is a Plymouth County town of 61,217 people (2020 Census) on Cape Cod Bay, about 40 miles south of Boston, and the largest municipality in Massachusetts by area. Founded by the Mayflower Pilgrims in 1620, it is one of the county's two seats. About 71 percent of its homes are detached single-family houses. Route 3 serves the town with six exits, and Plymouth's own commuter rail station has been suspended since 2021, so the nearest active stop is Kingston.
overview: The Mayflower Pilgrims settled here in December 1620, and Plymouth served as the capital of Plymouth Colony until 1691. The old town center keeps that story close to the water: Plymouth Rock under its 1921 portico in Pilgrim Memorial State Park, the Mayflower II at the State Pier, Cole's Hill, and Burial Hill above Leyden Street, where the Pilgrims built a fort in 1621 and 1622. Pilgrim Hall, opened in 1824 on Court Street, is the oldest public museum in the United States in continuous operation. Plymouth Colony merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691, and the town governed itself by open town meeting from 1622 until voters adopted a representative town meeting in 1953.

Beyond downtown the town spreads across about 96 square miles of land. North Plymouth grew around the Plymouth Cordage Company, once the largest maker of rope and twine in the world, and much of its multifamily housing evolved from mill housing; the company closed in 1964. West Plymouth filled with subdivisions in the 1970s, and South Plymouth drew new growth from the 1980s. Inland, Myles Standish State Forest has ponds and pine and oak woods, while Manomet and Ellisville Harbor sit along the Cape Cod Bay shore. Plymouth Beach, about three miles long, is the largest of the town's nine public beaches, and the town also holds the 81-foot National Monument to the Forefathers, dedicated in 1889.

Detached single-family homes make up 71.1 percent of Plymouth's housing units, according to its 2024 Housing Production Plan, and the town grew from 25,058 units in 2010 to 28,353 in 2021, with most new building expected in its rural areas. Because Plymouth is adjacent to Kingston, which has a commuter rail station, the state's MBTA Communities law treats it as an adjacent community that must zone for at least 2,807 multifamily units by right. On January 24, 2024, the Planning Board voted 4 to 0 to recommend Article 18 to the April 2024 Annual Town Meeting: a Multifamily Overlay District with four subdistricts, Cordage, Home Depot Drive, Plaza Way and The Pinehills, where, as drafted in January 2024, developments of ten or more units must make at least 10 percent of them affordable. The state now lists Plymouth as compliant. Cordage Park also has a Chapter 40R district, capped at 675 units.

housing.text: Plymouth's 2024 Housing Production Plan reports that detached single-family homes make up 71.1 percent of housing units, with attached single-family homes another 7.4 percent. As of 2021, 80.9 percent of occupied homes were owner-occupied, and the town's housing units grew from 25,058 in 2010 to 28,353 in 2021. The plan expects most new residential development in the town's rural areas, with recent projects in the south and at Cordage Park in the north.

villages.name: North Plymouth
villages.line: A waterfront village around the former Plymouth Cordage Company, whose multifamily housing largely evolved from mill housing.

villages.name: Manomet
villages.line: A seaside village named for a Wampanoag village once among the Manomet Ponds, with White Horse Beach and Stage Point.

villages.name: West Plymouth
villages.line: The hilly, forested western section, where single-family subdivisions grew in the 1970s.

villages.name: Cedarville
villages.line: A neighborhood in the southeast of town, linked to Manomet by a local bus route.

villages.name: South Plymouth
villages.line: The southern part of town, which has drawn new residential growth since the 1980s; the Housing Production Plan notes recent projects there.

commute.text: Plymouth station at Cordage Park was suspended indefinitely on April 5, 2021, and is not on the current Kingston Line timetable, so the nearest active stop is Kingston station at 134 Marion Drive, with trains to South Station. Route 3 runs through town with six exits, and Route 44 ends in Plymouth. GATRA runs local routes including the Liberty, Freedom, Mayflower and Manomet Links, Plymouth & Brockton buses run to Boston and Hyannis, and a seasonal ferry sails from State Wharf to Provincetown.

places.name: Pilgrim Memorial State Park
places.line: The waterfront park at 79 Water Street with Plymouth Rock under its portico, the Mayflower II, Cole's Hill Burial Ground and views of Plymouth Harbor.

places.name: Plimoth Patuxet Museums
places.line: A living history museum at 137 Warren Avenue with the Historic Patuxet Homesite, a re-created 17th-century English Village, the Plimoth Grist Mill and Mayflower II.

places.name: Pilgrim Hall Museum
places.line: A granite museum at 75 Court Street, designed by Alexander Parris and opened in 1824, holding a Plymouth Colony collection.

places.name: Burial Hill
places.line: The hillside burying ground off School Street, with marked graves from 1680, including that of Governor William Bradford.

places.name: Myles Standish State Forest
places.line: A DCR forest of pine and oak with 13 miles of hiking trails, 35 miles of equestrian trails, camping and swimming at College Pond.

places.name: Ellisville Harbor State Park
places.line: A Cape Cod Bay shore park at 1861 State Road with a beach, meadows, red pine forest and harbor seals offshore in winter.

places.name: Plymouth Beach
places.line: The largest of the town's nine public beaches, roughly three miles long.

places.name: National Monument to the Forefathers
places.line: An 81-foot monument to the Pilgrims, dedicated in 1889.

history.text: The Mayflower Pilgrims founded the settlement in December, and Plymouth served as Plymouth Colony's capital until 1691.
After the fall harvest, the Pilgrims held a thanksgiving celebration with Wampanoag guests, remembered as the First Thanksgiving.
The Plymouth Cordage Company was founded in North Plymouth; it operated for more than 140 years before closing in 1964.
The National Monument to the Forefathers, 81 feet tall, was dedicated.
The present portico over Plymouth Rock was built.

ot_record.name: Braintree
headline: Saltbox houses on Washington Street,
and a station where three rail lines meet.
ot_record.answer: Braintree is a Norfolk County community of 39,143 people (2020 Census), about ten miles south of Boston, where I-93 and Route 3 meet. Most of its housing, 64 percent, is single-family detached homes. Braintree station on Ivory Street is served by the Red Line and two commuter rail lines, and the Greenbush Line stops at Weymouth Landing/East Braintree on the town line. It is legally a city with a mayor and council, though it keeps the name Town of Braintree.
overview: Captain Wollaston first colonized the area, then called Mount Wollaston, in 1625. Braintree was colonized in 1635 and incorporated in 1640, and the old town once took in what are now Quincy, Randolph and Holbrook; Quincy left in 1792 and Randolph in 1793. The town counts John Adams, John Quincy Adams, John Hancock and General Sylvanus Thayer among those born in Old Braintree. The Braintree iron forge of 1646 is thought to have stood near Elm and Middle Streets, and water power on the Monatiquot River drew mills to South Braintree in the 1820s. The Old Colony railroad arrived there in 1845, making South Braintree a rail junction, while East Braintree grew at the head of navigation on the Fore River. Braintree became a city with a mayor and council in 2007, though it keeps the name Town of Braintree.

Washington Street carries much of the town's older fabric, including the Thayer Birthplace, built in 1720, and the Asa French House, built about 1699, both now in the town's historic district. A 1979 state survey found especially large concentrations of center-entrance Cape houses in East Braintree, along the Monatiquot, and Braintree Highlands was laid out as a street grid in the 1870s but built up mainly in the 20th century. Five Corners, on West Street, became a commercial junction after Route 128 reached it in 1931. Open space includes the Town Forest, Sunset Lake, Smith Beach, the Cranberry Pond Conservation District and Pond Meadow Park, shared with Weymouth, along with an 18-hole public golf course. The town site describes established neighborhoods, small clusters of new homes and several condominium complexes.

A 2024 town feasibility study counts 64 percent of Braintree's housing units as single-family detached and about 74 percent as owner-occupied. As a rapid transit community under the state's MBTA Communities law, Braintree had to zone for at least 3,769 multifamily units by right, 25 percent of its 15,077 year-round units. In December 2023 the Town Council voted 6 to 2 to create four overlay districts covering about 204 acres: two near Braintree station (one taking in the Marketplace at Braintree on Grossman Drive), one off Hancock and Pearl Streets in South Braintree and one beside Weymouth Landing/East Braintree, which the town's November 2023 compliance model put at 3,922 units. Projects of ten or more units must make at least 10 percent of them affordable, and the state lists Braintree as compliant. In March 2026 the Planning Board approved the site plan for 752 apartments on the former Armstrong World Industries plant off Plain Street, beside the restored Monatiquot River.

housing.text: A 2024 town feasibility study reports that 64 percent of Braintree's housing is single-family detached units and that about 74 percent of units are owner-occupied. Only 12 percent of units are studios or one-bedrooms. The study counts a 5.42 percent increase in housing units from 2010 to 2020. The town also lists several condominium complexes among its housing.

villages.name: South Braintree
villages.line: The old industrial center along the Monatiquot River, where mills developed in the 1820s and the Old Colony railroad made a junction in 1845.

villages.name: East Braintree
villages.line: The area at the head of navigation on the Fore River, with Colonial-era Capes along the Monatiquot; its rail stop is Weymouth Landing/East Braintree.

villages.name: Braintree Highlands
villages.line: Laid out as a street grid in the 1870s and built up in the 20th century; the Thayer house was built here in 1720 before its move.

villages.name: Washington Street
villages.line: The town's civic spine since a town house was built midway along it in 1829, with the Thayer and French houses and Town Hall.

villages.name: Five Corners
villages.line: The junction on West Street in South Braintree reached by Route 128 in 1931, where commercial building and gas stations grew up along the former highway.

villages.name: Elm and Middle Streets
villages.line: High ground north of the Monatiquot River where the earliest settlement grew, and the likely site of the Braintree iron forge of 1646.

commute.text: Braintree station, at 197 Ivory Street, has a Red Line platform, a commuter rail platform for the Kingston and Fall River/New Bedford lines to South Station, a busway and a 1,197-space garage. Weymouth Landing/East Braintree, on the Greenbush Line, sits on the town line with Weymouth. The seasonal CapeFLYER stops at Braintree on summer weekends on its way to Hyannis. I-93 and Route 3 meet in town.

places.name: Pond Meadow Park
places.line: A 320-acre park shared with Weymouth, opened in 1976, with a two-mile paved loop around a 20-acre pond and unpaved trails branching off it.

places.name: General Sylvanus Thayer Birthplace
places.line: A 1720 farmhouse at 786 Washington Street, birthplace of the West Point superintendent, moved here in 1958 and listed on the National Register in 1974.

places.name: Asa French House
places.line: A house built about 1699 at 766 Washington Street, now owned by the Braintree Historical Society.

places.name: Thayer Public Library
places.line: The town library across from Town Hall, on land acquired in 1953 and rebuilt in 1997, with more than 125,000 items.

places.name: Blue Hills Reservation
places.line: A DCR reservation of more than 7,000 acres and 125 miles of trails, with a paved accessible path on Old Route 128 off West Street in Braintree.

places.name: Sunset Lake and the Town Forest
places.line: Two of the town's recreation areas, along with Smith Beach and the Cranberry Pond Conservation District.

places.name: Monatiquot River and Rock Falls
places.line: The river through South Braintree, where removal of the Armstrong and Ames Pond dams began in 2023; a fishway bypass around Rock Falls is meant to let river herring reach Great Pond Reservoir for the first time in about 200 years.

history.text: Braintree, colonized in 1635, was incorporated as a town.
Quincy was incorporated from the original town, followed by Randolph in 1793.
The Old Colony railroad reached South Braintree, which became a rail junction as branches followed to Fall River in 1846 and Randolph in 1866.
The murders that led to the Sacco and Vanzetti trial took place in Braintree.
Braintree was incorporated as a city with a mayor and council form of government, and elected its first mayor that November.

faq.a: In four MBTA Communities overlay districts the Town Council adopted in December 2023, covering about 204 acres near Braintree station, off Hancock and Pearl Streets in South Braintree and beside Weymouth Landing/East Braintree. Projects of ten or more units must make at least 10 percent of them affordable, and the state lists Braintree as compliant with the law.

communities.title: Barnstable
communities.excerpt: Barnstable is the seat of Barnstable County, a town of 48,916 people (2020 Census) made up of seven villages that run from Cape Cod Bay to Nantucket Sound.

ot_record.name: Barnstable
headline: Seven villages between two shores,
from the Great Marsh to the Hyannis ferries.
ot_record.answer: Barnstable is the seat of Barnstable County, a town of 48,916 people (2020 Census) made up of seven villages that run from Cape Cod Bay to Nantucket Sound. Detached single-family homes make up 84.8 percent of its residential properties, and the town's housing plan counts at least 23 percent of its housing units as second homes. Hyannis holds the town's transit links: the seasonal CapeFLYER train from Boston ends at the Hyannis Transportation Center, and ferries leave Hyannis for Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard. U.S. Route 6 crosses the town as a four-lane freeway.
overview: Bartholomew Gosnold explored this shore in 1602, and English settlers arrived on June 4, 1638, making Barnstable one of the first towns of Plymouth Colony; it was incorporated in 1639. The north side still follows the Old King's Highway, Route 6A, through Barnstable village and West Barnstable, where the 1644 house that forms the original part of the Sturgis Library is the oldest building housing a public library in the United States, and the Olde Colonial Courthouse recalls a 1774 protest led by James Otis and Samuel Adams. Behind them, Sandy Neck runs about six and a half miles along Cape Cod Bay, backed by salt marsh, with Sandy Neck Light at its tip.

The south side faces Nantucket Sound. Hyannis holds the historic Main Street, a large natural harbor and the ferry docks, along with Barnstable Municipal Airport and the Hyannis Transportation Center. West along Route 28, Centerville reaches Craigville Beach, Osterville keeps the Crosby boatbuilding story in its historical museum, and Cotuit sits on Cotuit Bay, the home water of the Cotuit oyster. Inland, Marstons Mills takes its name from Benjamin Marston's fulling mill and keeps a herring run, kettle ponds and a grass airfield dating to 1929. Hyannis is also home to Cape Cod Hospital, the largest medical facility on Cape Cod, and the Cape Cod Central Railroad runs seasonal excursions from there to Sandwich and Sagamore.

Barnstable's 2025 Housing Production Plan counts detached single-family homes as 84.8 percent of residential properties and at least 23 percent of housing units as second homes; rental housing is 24 percent of the stock. Multifamily and mixed-use buildings are allowed by right on only two percent of the town's net land area, and accessory dwelling units were recently allowed by right in all zoning districts. The town had 1,485 units on the state's Subsidized Housing Inventory, 6.73 percent of its 2020 year-round units, against a 10 percent goal. In Hyannis, the Town Council approved new Downtown Hyannis zoning on February 2, 2023, replacing the Hyannis Village districts with seven form-based and hybrid districts that allow buildings of up to four stories and are meant to allow compact housing by right. Barnstable is not one of the 177 MBTA communities.

housing.text: Barnstable's 2025 Housing Production Plan executive summary counts detached single-family homes as 84.8 percent of residential properties, and reports that at least 23 percent of the town's housing units are second homes. Hyannis holds about one-fifth of all housing units; single-family homes are 59 percent of its units, and most of its units are rented. The plan names town-owned sites in Marstons Mills, among others, for new year-round housing.

villages.name: Hyannis
villages.line: The largest village, with the historic Main Street, the harbor and ferry docks, the Hyannis Transportation Center and Barnstable Municipal Airport.

villages.name: Barnstable Village
villages.line: The north-side village along the Old King's Highway (Route 6A), with a working harbor, the county complex, the Sturgis Library and the Olde Colonial Courthouse.

villages.name: West Barnstable
villages.line: A northwestern village on Route 6A whose land is largely Sandy Neck, the Great Marsh and the West Barnstable Conservation Area, centered on the West Parish meetinghouse of 1717 to 1718.

villages.name: Centerville
villages.line: A south-side village with the Centerville Historic District, the Centerville Historical Museum and Craigville Beach in its Craigville neighborhood.

villages.name: Osterville
villages.line: A village facing Nantucket Sound, with West Bay, the Wianno neighborhood by East Bay and the Crosby boatbuilding tradition.

villages.name: Cotuit
villages.line: The village on Cotuit Bay, midway between Falmouth and Hyannis, where the Cotuit Kettleers play Cape Cod Baseball League games at Lowell Park.

villages.name: Marstons Mills
villages.line: An inland village on glacial plains, with the Marstons Mills River, a herring run, kettle ponds such as Mystic Lake and Hamblin Pond, and saltwater access only at Prince Cove.

rail.line: CapeFLYER (seasonal weekends, Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day)

commute.text: Barnstable has no year-round passenger rail; the nearest year-round MBTA Commuter Rail stations are Middleborough and Kingston. In summer, the CapeFLYER runs weekends only from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day between Boston's South Station and the Hyannis Transportation Center, with stops including Braintree, Brockton, Wareham Village, Buzzards Bay and Bourne. The Hyannis Transportation Center is also the terminal for Cape Cod Regional Transit Authority buses, including the Sealine to Falmouth and Woods Hole, and for Plymouth & Brockton and Peter Pan intercity buses. From Hyannis, the Steamship Authority runs year-round ferries to Nantucket and a seasonal high-speed passenger ferry, and Hy-Line runs passenger ferries to Nantucket and a seasonal catamaran to Martha's Vineyard. Barnstable Municipal Airport in Hyannis has scheduled flights to the islands and Boston. U.S. Route 6 crosses the town as a four-lane freeway, and Routes 132 and 149 link Route 6A to Route 28.

places.name: Sandy Neck
places.line: A public barrier beach about 6.5 miles long on Cape Cod Bay, backed by salt marsh, with Sandy Neck Light's 1857 brick tower at Beach Point.

places.name: John F. Kennedy Hyannis Museum
places.line: A museum at 397 Main Street, Hyannis, on President Kennedy, his family and their connection to Cape Cod; hours change by season.

places.name: Sturgis Library
places.line: A library at 3090 Main Street (Route 6A) in Barnstable Village whose building is the oldest structure housing a public library in the United States.

places.name: Osterville Historical Museum
places.line: A museum at 155 West Bay Road, founded in 1931, with the Cammett, Parker and Jelly houses and more than a dozen full-sized Crosby wooden boats.

places.name: Hyannis Harbor and Main Street
places.line: A large natural harbor, the Cape's largest recreational boating port, beside the historic downtown Main Street shopping district.

places.name: Lowell Park, Cotuit
places.line: The summer home field of the Cotuit Kettleers of the Cape Cod Baseball League.

places.name: Cahoon Museum of American Art
places.line: A museum in the Crocker house at 4676 Falmouth Road (Route 28) in Cotuit, with American art from the 18th century to the present, including the folk art and painted furniture of Ralph and Martha Cahoon.

places.name: West Parish Meetinghouse
places.line: The restored meetinghouse in West Barnstable, built after the church split into East and West parishes in 1717, and still home to the West Parish of Barnstable.

history.text: Bartholomew Gosnold became the first European to explore the area.
Settled on June 4, 1638, as one of the first towns of Plymouth Colony, Barnstable was incorporated the following September.
Protesters led by James Otis and Samuel Adams interrupted court proceedings at the Olde Colonial Courthouse, now a museum.
The Cape Cod Branch Railroad reached West Barnstable, and a depot was built in the village.
Barnstable adopted a council-manager charter and was incorporated as a city on April 11.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Barnstable, MA?

faq.q: Does Barnstable have commuter rail?

faq.q: Where do the island ferries leave from in Barnstable?
faq.a: From Hyannis. The Steamship Authority runs ferries to Nantucket year-round, plus a seasonal high-speed passenger ferry, and Hy-Line runs passenger ferries to Nantucket and a seasonal catamaran to Martha's Vineyard.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Barnstable, MA?
faq.a: According to the Massachusetts Division of Local Services, Barnstable's FY2026 residential property tax rate is $6.80 per $1,000 of assessed value, and commercial, industrial and personal property pay $5.94. Each property also pays its fire district's rate (FY2026, per $1,000: Barnstable $2.81, Cotuit $2.07, Centerville-Osterville-Marstons Mills $1.15, Hyannis $2.40 residential, West Barnstable $2.66) and a 3% Community Preservation surcharge on the town tax. faq.q: What has Barnstable changed in its zoning for housing?

ot_record.name: Falmouth
headline: A village green, a seaside bikeway,
and the ferry to the Vineyard at Woods Hole.
ot_record.answer: Falmouth is an Upper Cape town of 32,517 people (2020 Census) in Barnstable County, bordered by Buzzards Bay to the west and Vineyard Sound to the south. Its 2024 Housing Production Plan counts 22,817 housing units, about 86 percent of them detached single-family homes, with 30 percent counted as seasonal units. Falmouth has no rail station: Steamship Authority ferries leave Woods Hole for Martha's Vineyard, and buses link the town to Hyannis and to Boston and Logan Airport. The median single-family sale price was $804,000 in 2025, across 424 sales.
overview: English colonists settled Falmouth in 1660, and the town was incorporated in 1686. Its center has gathered around a triangular village green since 1756, when the meeting house moved there, and late Colonial and Federal houses still frame it with the 1796 First Congregational Church on its north side. Katharine Lee Bates, who wrote the words to "America the Beautiful", was born on Main Street in 1859. Woods Hole was raided by British forces in 1779, and the Falmouth Heights shore was bombarded by British frigates in the War of 1812. By 1872 the railroad had reached Falmouth and Woods Hole.

That rail line is now the Shining Sea Bikeway, 10.7 miles from Route 151 in North Falmouth to the Steamship Authority dock in Woods Hole, with a stretch along the water. Woods Hole is a working science village: the Marine Biological Laboratory dates to 1888 and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution to 1930, around the drawbridge at Eel Pond, with Nobska Light on the point above Vineyard Sound. Along the south shore, a run of closely spaced coastal ponds and necks leads east to the Waquoit Bay reserve, while West and North Falmouth face Buzzards Bay with harbors and public beaches such as Old Silver Beach.

The town's March 2024 Housing Production Plan counts 22,817 housing units in 2020, about 86 percent of them detached single-family homes and 30 percent counted as seasonal, with an estimated 62 percent in structures built before 1980. At 8.13 percent, Falmouth's Subsidized Housing Inventory is below the 10 percent Chapter 40B goal, and the plan sets a target of at least 80 affordable units a year, with strategies including pre-approved plans for detached accessory dwellings and housing on town-owned land. Town Meeting loosened the accessory dwelling bylaw in 2018, cutting the minimum lot size from 15,000 to 7,500 square feet, and since February 2, 2025 state law has allowed one accessory dwelling of up to 900 square feet (or half the main house, if smaller) by right in single-family zoning districts. Falmouth is not on the state's MBTA Communities list, although neighboring Bourne is, as an adjacent small town.

housing.text: Falmouth's March 2024 Housing Production Plan counts 22,817 housing units in 2020, up from 18,168 in 1990. An estimated 86 percent are detached single-family homes, and 70 percent are counted as year-round units, with 30 percent counted as seasonal; an estimated 62 percent are in structures built before 1980, and 8.13 percent count toward the state's Subsidized Housing Inventory. The plan aims to direct new housing to areas that are already developed and to maximize affordable units on town-owned land.

villages.name: Woods Hole
villages.line: The village at the southwestern tip of the Cape, around Eel Pond and its drawbridge, home to the Steamship Authority terminal, WHOI, the Marine Biological Laboratory and a USGS coastal and marine center.

villages.name: West Falmouth

villages.line: The south-shore area of necks between tidal ponds (Great, Green, Bournes and Eel ponds), with Hatchville to the north on Route 151 and Waquoit to the east on Waquoit Bay.

villages.line: The village between Falmouth Village and East Falmouth, crossed by Route 28; south of the road, a neck between Great Pond and Little Pond runs down to Vineyard Sound and holds the Maravista neighborhood.

rail.line: CapeFLYER (seasonal weekends, Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day, in neighboring Bourne)

commute.text: Falmouth has no rail station. The seasonal CapeFLYER, weekends only from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day, stops in neighboring Bourne and Buzzards Bay on its way between Boston's South Station and Hyannis. Peter Pan buses run from Logan Airport and downtown Boston to the Falmouth Bus Depot. The Cape Cod Regional Transit Authority's Sealine connects the Hyannis Transportation Center with Falmouth Center and the Woods Hole ferry docks along Route 28, and from late June to Labor Day the Whoosh Trolley runs from the Falmouth Mall through Falmouth Center to Woods Hole. Steamship Authority ferries to Martha's Vineyard leave Woods Hole year-round, and the seasonal, passenger-only Island Queen crosses from Falmouth Harbor to Oak Bluffs in about 35 minutes. Route 28 runs south from Bourne as the town's main road, and Route 151 crosses the north of town.

places.name: Shining Sea Bikeway
places.line: A 10.7-mile rail-trail from County Road (Route 151) in North Falmouth to the Steamship Authority on Crane Street in Woods Hole, named for a line of "America the Beautiful".

places.name: Nobska Light
places.line: A lighthouse on Nobska Road in Woods Hole, a station since 1828 with its present tower from 1876, overlooking Martha's Vineyard and Nonamesset Island.

places.name: Waquoit Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve
places.line: About 2,700 acres of open water, barrier beach, marsh and upland in East Falmouth, with trails, a visitor center and boat-access campsites on Washburn Island.

places.name: Falmouth Village Green

places.name: Woods Hole and Eel Pond

places.name: Old Silver Beach
places.line: A public beach on Buzzards Bay off Quaker Road in North Falmouth.

places.name: Highfield Hall and Beebe Woods
places.line: James Madison Beebe bought more than 700 acres in the late 1800s, after the railroad reached the Cape, and built Highfield Hall, now a museum; much of his former land is preserved as Beebe Woods, and the College Light Opera Company has played the Highfield Theatre every summer since 1969.

places.name: Spohr Gardens
places.line: About 6 acres of woodland garden at 45 Fells Road, with paths along Oyster Pond, open to the public free of charge.

history.text: First settled by English colonists in 1660, Falmouth was incorporated as a town.
The meeting house moved to the village green, which has been the town center since.
Katharine Lee Bates, author of "America the Beautiful", was born in Falmouth on August 12.
The railroad reached Falmouth and Woods Hole; its right-of-way later became the Shining Sea Bikeway.
The Marine Biological Laboratory was founded in Woods Hole, a village that had been a whaling station in the 1820s; the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution followed in 1930.

ot_record.name: New Bedford
headline: Cobblestones above the working harbor,
and the train back on Acushnet Avenue.
ot_record.answer: New Bedford is a Bristol County city of 101,079 people (2020 Census) on the Acushnet River where it meets Buzzards Bay. Its downtown waterfront is part of New Bedford Whaling National Historical Park, established in 1996. The Warren Group counted 401 single-family sales in 2025. Since March 24, 2025, the MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line has run from New Bedford and Church Street stations to Boston's South Station, and I-195 crosses the city.
overview: New Bedford was incorporated as a town in 1787 and became a city in 1847. In the first half of the 1800s it was one of the world's most important whaling ports, and in 1857 its harbor counted 329 vessels. The downtown historic district, 11 city blocks and part of a twelfth west of the waterfront, keeps Federal and Greek Revival buildings put up mostly between 1790 and 1855, including Seamen's Bethel and the 1836 U.S. Customhouse. Frederick Douglass settled in the city in 1838 and lived there until 1841.

When whaling faded, cotton mills took over, and the Wamsutta Mills were for a time the world's largest weaving plant. The housing that followed spreads out from downtown: the County Street Historic District, laid out in the 18th century, holds City Hall, the library and large houses in Greek Revival and Gothic Revival styles, while Acushnet Heights keeps wood-frame houses built for factory workers from the 1860s on. Buttonwood Park and its zoo sit to the west, and Fort Taber Park occupies Clark's Point, the city's southern tip on Buzzards Bay.

The state's MBTA Communities table counts 44,588 housing units in New Bedford in 2020, and the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 survey puts the owner-occupied share at 40.3 percent. In March 2023 the city published Building New Bedford, a housing plan that set a 90-day approval target for large multifamily projects, proposed smaller minimum lots and lower parking minimums (then two spaces per new unit), and proposed revisiting the rules on accessory dwellings, since detached ones were not then allowed. As a commuter rail community under the MBTA Communities law, the city needed multifamily zoning near its new stations: the City Council approved a transit-oriented district along Kings Highway, around Church Street station in the North End, in November 2024, and the state lists New Bedford as compliant as of October 21, 2026. A second overlay, the Clasky Common district along Purchase Street near New Bedford station, was proposed in early 2025.

housing.text: The state's MBTA Communities table counts 44,588 housing units in New Bedford in 2020, and the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 American Community Survey puts the owner-occupied share at 40.3 percent. The city's 2023 Building New Bedford plan counted 39,059 occupied units, 60.2 percent of them rented, and noted that triple-deckers are abundant and that surrounding towns have a higher share of single-family homes. Older neighborhoods mix 19th-century wood-frame houses with downtown commercial and mixed-use blocks, and The Warren Group recorded 401 single-family sales in 2025.

villages.name: Downtown and the Waterfront
villages.line: The historic district between Front, Elm and Commercial Streets and Acushnet Avenue, about 11 city blocks of Federal and Greek Revival buildings beside the harbor.

villages.name: County Street
villages.line: About 100 acres along County Street, roughly bounded by Acushnet, Page, Middle and Bedford Streets, with City Hall, the library and Greek Revival, Gothic Revival and Late Victorian buildings.

villages.name: Acushnet Heights
villages.line: About 20 acres around Clasky Common Park, bounded by Purchase, Linden and County Streets, with wood-frame houses built from the 1860s for factory workers and four 19th-century churches.

villages.name: Clark's Point
villages.line: The southernmost point of the city, where the Acushnet River meets Buzzards Bay, home to Fort Taber Park.

villages.name: Central New Bedford
villages.line: A 29-acre rectangle bounded by Acushnet Avenue and School, Middle and Sixth Streets, with 79 buildings, mostly commercial or mixed-use and largely Classical Revival or Romanesque Revival, including the 1908-10 Registry of Deeds and the 1915 Post Office.

villages.name: Howland Mill Village
villages.line: A 9.9-acre district roughly bounded by Bolton, Winsper and Hemlock Streets and Rockdale Avenue, with single-family cottages built in 1888-89 for the nearby Howland Mill on just two floor plans, and double-decker houses added in the 1920s.

rail.line: Fall River/New Bedford Line (New Bedford branch)

commute.text: Commuter rail returned on March 24, 2025, after a gap since 1958. New Bedford and Church Street stations sit on the New Bedford branch of the Fall River/New Bedford Line, which runs through East Taunton, Middleborough, Brockton and Quincy to Boston's South Station; sample outbound weekday trips on the current timetable take about 1 hour 40 to 45 minutes, and the timetable also shows weekend trains to New Bedford. Both stations are in fare zone 8 and have full high-level platforms; New Bedford station shares the Whale's Tooth lot with the SeaStreak ferry and has 150 spaces for rail riders, and Church Street station, in the North End off Church Street, has 355. I-195 crosses the city toward Providence and Wareham, Route 18 links it to the waterfront, and Route 140 runs north to Route 24 in Taunton. SRTA runs local buses, and SeaStreak ferries sail from New Bedford to Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket, with separate service to Cuttyhunk Island.

places.name: New Bedford Whaling National Historical Park
places.line: A fee-free national park in downtown New Bedford, with its visitor center at 33 William Street.

places.name: New Bedford Whaling Museum
places.line: Founded in 1903 by the Old Dartmouth Historical Society, at 18 Johnny Cake Hill.

places.name: Buttonwood Park Zoo
places.line: A city-owned, AZA-accredited zoo at 425 Hawthorn Street, with animals from five continents.

places.name: Fort Taber Park
places.line: A 47-acre park at Clark's Point with the 1857 stone fort, Endicott-era batteries and the Fort Taber/Fort Rodman military museum.

places.name: Seamen's Bethel
places.line: A white clapboard chapel in the downtown historic district, first built in 1832 and rebuilt after an 1867 fire.

places.name: Rotch-Jones-Duff House and Garden Museum
places.line: A house at 396 County Street, built in 1834 for whaling merchant William Rotch Jr. to Richard Upjohn's design on a one-acre block; a museum since 1983 and a National Historic Landmark since 2005.

places.name: Zeiterion Performing Arts Center
places.line: A downtown theater that opened on April 2, 1923 for vaudeville, passed to WHALE (the Waterfront Historic Area League) on December 31, 1981, was restored with WHALE funding for the first phase, and reopened on September 25, 1982; its facade was restored in 2014.

places.name: New Bedford Hurricane Barrier
places.line: Begun in October 1962 and dedicated on May 21, 1966, the barrier and its dikes run about 3.5 miles across the harbor and Clark's Cove, with a 150-foot navigation gate, and protect more than 1,400 acres in New Bedford, Fairhaven and Acushnet.

history.text: Incorporated as a town on February 23; it became a city on March 18, 1847.
Frederick Douglass settled in New Bedford, where he lived and worked on the wharves until 1841.
Construction of the harbor's hurricane barrier began in October; it went into operation in January 1966 and was dedicated on May 21, 1966.
The waterfront historic district was designated a National Historic Landmark on November 13.
Commuter rail service to Boston resumed on March 24, the first since 1958.

communities.title: Fall River
communities.excerpt: Fall River is a Bristol County city of 94,000 people (2020 Census) on the Taunton River and Mount Hope Bay, at the Rhode Island line.

ot_record.name: Fall River
headline: Granite mills on a falling river,
a battleship at the foot of the hill.
ot_record.answer: Fall River is a Bristol County city of 94,000 people (2020 Census) on the Taunton River and Mount Hope Bay, at the Rhode Island line. It grew into a leading U.S. textile city in the 1800s, and its housing still includes many 19th-century triple-deckers. The Warren Group counted 300 single-family sales in 2025. Since March 24, 2025, Fall River Depot station has linked the city to Boston's South Station on the MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line, and I-195 and Route 24 meet here.
overview: Fall River separated from Freetown as a town in 1803, spent about 30 years named Troy, and took back its name in 1834; it became a city in 1854. The name comes from the Quequechan River, believed to mean 'falling river' in Wampanoag. A fire in July 1843 destroyed much of the town center, and the city motto, 'We'll Try', dates from the rebuilding. Mills followed the river's drop to the bay, and by 1868 the city had passed Lowell as the leading U.S. textile city. The 1847 Metacomet Mill is its oldest surviving textile mill.

I-195 divides the city into the North End and the South End. North of the highway, the Highlands ridge keeps houses from about 1840 to 1925 in Greek Revival, Italianate, Second Empire and Queen Anne styles, along with North Park, designed by the Olmsted Brothers. Below it, the Lower Highlands mixes Federal and Greek Revival houses with late-19th-century multiunit worker housing. On the waterfront, Battleship Cove and Fall River Heritage State Park sit beside the Braga Bridge, and to the south Kennedy Park, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, slopes down to Mount Hope Bay.

The 2020 Census counted 44,346 housing units in Fall River, and the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 survey puts the owner-occupied share at 35.3 percent. The city's Waterfront Transit-Oriented Development district, created in 2011 along the Taunton River, already set a minimum multifamily density of four units and allowed mixed uses; to meet the MBTA Communities law the City Council extended it north from Davol Street to North Main Street and from Walnut Street north to Wayland Street, and the state lists Fall River as compliant as of October 21, 2026. MassDOT has been replacing the Route 79 expressway on the waterfront with a grid of surface streets and a narrower, rebuilt Davol Street (the work was nearing completion in November 2025), and on July 24, 2026 it opened bidding to develop about 20 acres of former highway land on the river beside Fall River Depot, which the state says could support more than 1,000 homes; proposals were due October 21, 2026.

housing.text: Fall River's mill boom housed workers in thousands of wood-frame, multi-family tenements, usually three-floor triple-deckers with up to six apartments, and mill companies built more than 12,000 units. The 2020 Census counted 44,346 housing units, 7.5 percent of them vacant. The Highlands and Lower Highlands keep older single-family and Victorian houses, and The Warren Group recorded 300 single-family sales in 2025.

villages.name: The Highlands
villages.line: A historic district on a ridge above the Taunton River and Mount Hope Bay, with more than 300 structures built mostly between 1840 and 1925 and the Olmsted Brothers' North Park.

ot_record.name: Pittsfield
headline: A county seat around Park Square,
with two lakes and a state forest at its edges.
ot_record.answer: Pittsfield is a city of 43,927 people (2020 Census) and the seat of Berkshire County. A city housing analysis describes its homes as mostly single-family houses and small two- and three-unit buildings, and The Warren Group counted 434 single-family sales in 2025. Amtrak's Lake Shore Limited stops at the Joseph Scelsi Intermodal Transportation Center, and the seasonal Berkshire Flyer runs from there to New York. US 7 and US 20 meet in the city, and the Massachusetts Turnpike is about 10 miles south in Lee.
overview: Settlement here dates to 1752, and the plantation of Pontoosuc was organized in 1753 before being incorporated as a town in 1761 and named for William Pitt. Park Square was laid out in 1790 on donated land, and the Old Town Hall, the county courthouse, the Berkshire Athenaeum and the First Church of Christ still face it. Late in the 19th century downtown pushed north along North Street, helped by an 1891 trolley line. In 1890 William Stanley Jr. founded the Stanley Electric Manufacturing Company here, and General Electric bought it in 1903. Pittsfield became a city in 1891.

Water and woods frame the city. Onota Lake, 617 acres and owned by the city, and Pontoosuc Lake are used for swimming, boating and fishing, and Pittsfield State Forest covers 11,000 acres with Berry Pond and 30 miles of trails. Herman Melville finished Moby-Dick at Arrowhead, his home on Holmes Road from 1850 to 1863. On West Housatonic Street, Hancock Shaker Village keeps 20 historic buildings, including a round stone barn from 1826. Downtown, the Colonial Theatre of 1903 reopened after restoration in 2006, and the Berkshire Museum, founded by Zenas Crane in 1903, holds more than 40,000 objects.

Pittsfield's homes are mostly older single-family houses and two- and three-unit buildings; the 2020 Census counted 21,738 housing units. On April 13, 2021, the City Council replaced the 2004 Downtown Arts Overlay District with a Downtown Creative District, which requires 20% of a building's units to be affordable but allows a waiver. In February 2025 the council allowed one accessory dwelling unit by right on any property with a one- or two-family house. One downtown conversion pairs the state's Housing Development Incentive Program with a local tax exemption: the former Berkshire County Savings Bank at 24 North Street is planned as Park Square Residences, 23 mixed-income apartments, and on July 9, 2026 it was reported to have received $4 million in state tax credits under that program. In August 2026 the Berkshire Regional Planning Commission began a housing production plan for the city, due to the state in May 2027.

housing.text: A 2009 city housing analysis describes Pittsfield's housing stock as relatively old, made up mainly of single-family homes and small multifamily buildings of two or three units, and counted 21,633 units citywide in 2008. In the Westside and Morningside neighborhoods next to downtown, more than 80% of homes were built before 1969, and many larger houses from the 1890s to 1930s have been divided into apartments.

communities.title: Great Barrington
communities.excerpt: Great Barrington is a Berkshire County town of 7,172 people (2020 Census) in the Housatonic River valley.

ot_record.name: Great Barrington
headline: A Main Street on the Housatonic,
and Monument Mountain up Route 7.
ot_record.answer: Great Barrington is a Berkshire County town of 7,172 people (2020 Census) in the Housatonic River valley. US 7 runs through its center as Main Street, and the town also takes in the villages of Housatonic and Van Deusenville. There is no passenger rail station in town; BRTA buses run to Lee and to Pittsfield, where Amtrak stops. The Warren Group counted 77 single-family sales in Great Barrington in 2025.
overview: The Mahican name for this stretch of the river was Mahaiwe, "the place downstream." Colonists settled here in 1726, the area served as the north parish of Sheffield from 1742, and it was incorporated as Great Barrington in 1761. In 1774 local colonists forced the Berkshire County court to close in protest of British policy, and in March 1886 William Stanley's alternating current system lit 23 businesses along Main Street. That Main Street still carries US 7 through the central village, where the Mahaiwe Theater opened in 1905 and reopened in 2005 as a performing arts center.

North of the center, the village of Housatonic grew in the early 1800s around textile and paper mills on the river; Monument Mills, which had 500 employees at its peak, closed in 1956, and the mill buildings are listed on the National Register. Monument Mountain rises along Route 7, with 503 acres and a 1,642-foot summit kept by The Trustees. To the east, East Mountain holds Ski Butternut and a state forest crossed by the Appalachian Trail. The Housatonic River Walk follows the river through downtown, and the W. E. B. Du Bois Boyhood Homesite, a National Historic Landmark, lies on the road to South Egremont.

Great Barrington's housing ranges from the Taconic and West Avenues Historic District south of downtown, where about two-thirds of the buildings date from 1890 to 1910, to recent nonprofit rentals. The Community Development Corporation of South Berkshire had Bentley Apartments, 45 affordable units on a former log-home factory site at 100 Bridge Street, under construction by February 2020, and with Way Finders opened Windrush Commons, 49 rental units in five buildings at 910 South Main Street, in June 2023. In December 2025 the state found the town eligible for its Seasonal Communities designation; the town planner told Town Meeting that seasonal units make up 12.71 percent of the housing stock. Voters accepted the designation in May 2026, giving the town up to 24 months to adopt any required zoning changes, and in an advisory vote declined, 94 to 31, to urge a residential tax exemption.

housing.text: Seasonal use shapes Great Barrington's housing. In December 2025 the Commonwealth identified the town as eligible for its Seasonal Communities designation, whose criteria include the share of housing units used for seasonal, recreational or occasional use. Voters at the Annual Town Meeting that opened on May 2, 2026 accepted the designation, which does not change local regulations by itself, and the Selectboard and Planning Board scheduled a joint meeting on related zoning changes for June 1, 2026.

villages.name: Risingdale

commute.text: Great Barrington has no passenger rail station. The Berkshire Regional Transit Authority runs Route 21 between Great Barrington and Lee and the Route 921 express between Great Barrington and Pittsfield, where Amtrak's Lake Shore Limited stops and the seasonal Berkshire Flyer runs to New York. US 7 is Main Street through the center, Route 23 crosses town west to east, and Route 183 serves the east side and Housatonic. The nearest interstate is the Massachusetts Turnpike (I-90). The rail line through town is the Berkshire Line, which the MassDOT Board voted in July 2014 to buy for future passenger service between New York and the Berkshires, with freight service to continue; passenger trains to Great Barrington ended in 1971, and their return remains a proposal. BRTA buses are fare-free through June 2027.

places.name: Monument Mountain
places.line: A 503-acre Trustees reservation on Route 7 with three trails to the 1,642-foot Peeskawso Peak, where Hawthorne and Melville once spent an afternoon.

places.name: Mahaiwe Performing Arts Center
places.line: The theater at 14 Castle Street opened on September 26, 1905, and reopened after restoration on May 29, 2005.

places.name: W. E. B. Du Bois Boyhood Homesite
places.line: A 5-acre National Historic Landmark (1976) on Routes 23 and 41, stewarded by UMass Amherst, with a path to a kiosk, a memorial boulder and the old house's foundation.

places.name: Housatonic River Walk
places.line: A national recreation trail along the river in downtown, a project of the Great Barrington Land Conservancy, open free in daylight from spring through fall.

places.name: Ski Butternut
places.line: A ski area on East Mountain with 22 trails and about 1,000 feet of vertical drop.

places.name: Lake Mansfield
places.line: A town-owned lake of about 30 acres, about a mile from downtown, with a swimming beach lifeguarded in summer, a 0.9-mile crushed-stone trail and a boat launch for canoes, kayaks and paddleboards; work on its parking, paths and play areas was substantially completed in November 2024.

places.name: Mason Library
places.line: The town's main library at 231 Main Street, opened in 1913; the stone base of an Alaskan totem pole placed on its side lawn in 1917 remains.

history.text: First settled by colonists, in the area the Mahican called Mahaiwe.
Incorporated as Great Barrington, after nearly two decades as the north parish of Sheffield.
Local colonists forced the temporary closure of the Berkshire County court in protest of British policy.
W. E. B. Du Bois was born in Great Barrington on February 23; he spent the first five years of his life at what is now the Du Bois Boyhood Homesite.
In March, William Stanley's alternating current lighting system lit 23 businesses along Main Street.

faq.q: Does Great Barrington have train service?
faq.a: No passenger rail station is located in Great Barrington. Passenger trains to Great Barrington ended in 1971; the MassDOT Board voted in 2014 to buy the Berkshire Line through town for future passenger service to New York, but that service remains a proposal. BRTA's Route 921 express bus connects the town with Pittsfield, where Amtrak's Lake Shore Limited stops and the seasonal Berkshire Flyer runs to New York (in 2026, Fridays and Sundays from June 12 to September 19).

faq.a: According to the Massachusetts Division of Local Services, Great Barrington's FY2026 residential property tax rate is $13.24 per $1,000 of assessed value, the same rate for all property classes. Great Barrington did not apply a residential exemption in FY2026; a January 2026 Selectboard presentation modeled adopting one, and at the May 2026 Town Meeting an advisory article urging the Selectboard to adopt it failed, 94 to 31. The Selectboard decides at its annual tax classification hearing, so check with the Assessors' Office for later years.

faq.q: What does the Seasonal Communities designation mean for Great Barrington?
faq.a: The Commonwealth found the town eligible in December 2025, and Annual Town Meeting voters accepted the designation in May 2026. It does not change local rules by itself; the town has up to 24 months to adopt any required zoning amendments, and the designation may open tools such as year-round occupancy restrictions, a year-round housing trust fund and zoning flexibility for undersized lots and tiny homes.
